notes.name: Achalpur
notes.note: Formerly Ellichpur, Amravati district, Maharashtra. Annexed by the Delhi Sultanate in the early 14th century and made a provincial seat. The capital of Berar through the sultanate centuries, the least studied of the five Deccan successor states.

notes.name: Adam
notes.note: Kuhi tehsil, Nagpur district, Maharashtra, in the Wainganga basin of eastern Vidarbha. A long sequence from the Chalcolithic through the megalithic and early historic periods to the Satavahana and Vakataka centuries. The site that gave the Asmaka mahajanapada a physical location.

notes.name: Adamgadh
notes.note: Madhya Pradesh, in the Narmada valley on the northern edge of the Satpuras. Lower and Middle Palaeolithic in the basal levels. One of the few sites in central India to preserve an unbroken sequence from the Palaeolithic through the Mesolithic into the food-producing stage.

notes.name: Adichanallur
notes.note: Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu. An urn-burial field excavated by Alexander Rea (ASI, 1899-1905) and again by T. Satyamurthy (ASI, 2003-05). The largest and earliest-excavated urn-burial site in Tamil Nadu, and the bridge between the iron age and the Sangam age.

notes.name: Adiyala
notes.note: Located in the Potwar region (West Punjab, Pakistan). Lower Palaeolithic (associated with the Sohanian / Sohan Valley pebble tool tradition). The site yielded characteristic Lower Palaeolithic core tools, including handaxes, choppers, and edged pebble tools.

notes.name: Agra Fort
notes.note: On the right bank of the Yamuna at Agra, Uttar Pradesh. A Lodi fort rebuilt in red sandstone by Akbar between 1565 and 1573. The whole evolution of Mughal architecture inside one enclosure, the clearest single site for the Akbar-to-Shah Jahan transition.

notes.name: Ahar
notes.note: On the outskirts of Udaipur, Rajasthan. Dated about 2100-1500 BCE. The type site of one of the three great Chalcolithic cultures of Rajasthan. The diagnostic pottery is a black-and-red ware with linear and dotted designs painted on in white.

notes.name: Ahichhatra
notes.note: Ahichchhatra (modern Ramnagar), Bareilly district, Uttar Pradesh. The site at which Painted Grey Ware was first identified. The type site of the PGW culture and one of its largest settlements, with a sequence running unbroken into the early historic city.

notes.name: Ahmednagar
notes.note: Western Maharashtra, on the Sina river in the upper Godavari basin. Capital of the Nizam Shahi sultanate. The Deccan sultanate that produced Malik Ambar, the administrator and general whose methods the Marathas inherited.

notes.name: Ahraura Minor Rock edict
notes.note: Mirzapur district, Uttar Pradesh. C. 258-257 BCE. The one version of Minor Rock Edict I that appears to mention relics of the Buddha. Minor Rock Edict I is Ashoka's personal statement: he has been a lay follower (upasaka) for more than two and a half years.

notes.name: Aihole
notes.note: Bagalkot district, Karnataka, on the left bank of the Malaprabha. Temple building spans c. 450-750 CE. The cradle of Indian temple architecture, the workshop in which Nagara and Dravida forms were tried out.

notes.name: Ajanta Caves
notes.note: Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar) district, Maharashtra. Thirty caves in two phases separated by some five centuries. The only place where Indian painting of the classical age survives in quantity. The paintings are not true fresco but tempera on a dry ground of mud.

notes.name: Ajmer(Hakra Basin)
notes.note: Situated in the Thar Desert region around Ajmer and the Budha Pushkar / Hokra lake basins in Rajasthan. Multi-layered sequence covering the Lower, Middle, and Upper Palaeolithic phases. The Budha Pushkar and Hokra basins provide a continuous sequence of prehistoric human occupation from the Lower Palaeolithic onwards.

notes.name: Ajmer Sharif
notes.note: Rajasthan. The dargah of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti. The principal Sufi shrine in India, and the institutional centre of the Chishti order. The Chishtis are defined by what they refused: state office, land grants and royal stipends.

notes.name: Akhnoor
notes.note: Jammu district, Jammu and Kashmir. The standing fort was begun by Mian Tej Singh in 1762 and completed under Raja Alam Singh about 1802. The northernmost extension of the Harappan world, and a Kushana-period Buddhist establishment in the Jammu hills.

notes.name: Akota
notes.note: A mound now inside Vadodara on the west bank of the Vishvamitri, Gujarat. Ranging from the late 5th or 6th century to the 12th century CE. The largest and earliest sequence of Jaina metal images in western India, the dated series against which all later Svetambara bronzes are measured.

notes.name: Alamgirpur
notes.note: Meerut district, western Uttar Pradesh, on the left bank of the Hindon. Period I is late Harappan, c. 1900-1400 BCE. Marks the eastern limit of the Harappan world, in the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab, and the point where the Harappan and PGW sequences meet.

notes.name: Alchi gompa Monastery
notes.note: Leh district, Ladakh. Founded in the late 10th or early 11th century. The oldest surviving wall paintings in Ladakh, and the last substantial body of Kashmiri Buddhist art anywhere, Kashmir's own having been destroyed.

notes.name: Allahabad
notes.note: The Allahabad (Prayagraj) pillar. C. 240s BCE. The most heavily inscribed object in Indian history, one pillar carrying Mauryan, Gupta and Mughal records, eighteen centuries apart. The Queen's Edict is the only Ashokan record to name a queen: it directs that the gifts of the second queen Karuvaki.

notes.name: Allahdino
notes.note: About 40 km east of Karachi in Sindh. A single-period mature Harappan village, c. 2500-2000 BCE. The classic small Harappan village, no citadel, no wall, which nonetheless carries the full urban artefact repertoire and startling wealth.

notes.name: Alwarturanagri - Nammavalar
notes.note: Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu, on the Thamirabarani river in the southern Pandya country. Generally placed in the 9th century CE. The central figure of Tamil Vaishnava bhakti, and the poet whose work Srivaishnavism treats as scripture.

notes.name: Amarkantak
notes.note: Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh. A group of some sixteen stone temples of the Kalachuri period. A river-source tirtha whose sanctity rests on hydrography rather than on any dynasty, the point where the Narmada is born.

notes.name: Amber
notes.note: Amer, about 11 km north of Jaipur, Rajasthan. Taken from the Meenas and held from the 12th century. The seat of the first Rajput house to ally with the Mughals, and the architectural record of what that alliance produced.

notes.name: Amravati or Dharanikota
notes.note: Amaravati with the adjoining fortified mound of Dharanikota, Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh. Dharanikota (ASI, R. Subrahmanyam, 1962-65) opens with an NBPW level of c. 400-300 BCE behind a mud rampart. A stratified NBPW level lying directly under a Satavahana capital.

notes.name: Amri
notes.note: Dadu district, Sindh, Pakistan. Four periods. The type-site of the Amri-Nal culture. Period I has mud-brick houses with small cellular compartments, usually interpreted as storage or granary bases.

notes.name: Anangpur
notes.note: In the Badarpur hills of the Aravalli quartzite ridge immediately south of Delhi (Faridabad district, Haryana). Lower Palaeolithic. Marking this as a large Lower Palaeolithic habitation-cum-factory site.

notes.name: Anjira
notes.note: In the Surab valley of Kalat district, Balochistan, Pakistan. A Chalcolithic settlement of roughly the 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. The reference sequence for central Balochistan, and a demonstration that prehistoric Balochistan was a mosaic of regional cultures rather than one.

notes.name: Apegaon - Janeshwar
notes.note: Paithan taluk, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra, on the Godavari. Jnaneshwar, or Dnyaneshwar, c. 1275-1296, wrote under the Yadavas of Devagiri. The founder of the Varkari tradition and the writer who made Marathi a language of philosophy.

notes.name: Arikamedu
notes.note: On the Ariyankuppam river about 4 km south of Puducherry town. Occupied from about the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE. The type-site of Indo-Roman trade, and the site whose reinterpretation changed how that trade is understood.

notes.name: Armamalai Caves
notes.note: Near Vellore in the Palar basin of northern Tamil Nadu. A Jaina cave shrine with paintings assigned to about the 8th century CE. A rare surviving example of Jaina cave painting in northern Tamil Nadu, and evidence of long monastic use of one shelter.

notes.name: Atiya Jame Masjid
notes.note: The Atia Jame Masjid at Atia, Delduar upazila, Tangail district, Bangladesh. Built in 1609 CE by Sa'id Khan Panni. A compact demonstration that Islamic architecture in Bengal is a regional idiom rather than an imported one.

notes.name: Atranji Khera
notes.note: Etah district, Uttar Pradesh, on the left bank of the Kali Nadi. Period I OCP, Period II Black and Red Ware, Period III PGW. The site at which a distinct BRW phase in the doab was first recognised, and the best evidence anywhere for PGW-age iron technology.

notes.name: Attirapakkam
notes.note: In the Kortallayar river basin, Tiruvallur district, about 60 km north-west of Chennai. Middle and Upper Palaeolithic in sequence. One of the richest and best-dated Palaeolithic sites in India. Acheulian tools were recovered from a 4 m thick clay deposit, the artefacts.

notes.name: Ayodhya
notes.note: Ayodhya, formerly Faizabad, district, Uttar Pradesh. Period I is NBPW. One of the sites that pushes the beginning of NBPW back before 600 BCE. NBPW occurs with a grey ware bearing linear designs.

notes.name: Badami
notes.note: Ancient Vatapi, Bagalkot district, Karnataka. Capital of the Early Chalukyas from c. 540 CE. The dated anchor of Deccan rock-cut architecture, and the Chalukya capital that Narasimhavarman I burnt. Cave 3, the largest and finest, is Vaishnava: a colossal Trivikrama, Varaha.

notes.name: Badrinath
notes.note: Chamoli district, Uttarakhand. A Vishnu shrine named in the Vishnu and Skanda Puranas and sung by the Alwars as a Divya Desam. One of the Char Dham, and the clearest surviving case of a pilgrimage network binding the subcontinent together.

notes.name: Bagalkot
notes.note: Northern Karnataka, in the Malaprabha-Ghataprabha basin of the Krishna system. Lower to Middle Palaeolithic. An early-to-middle Palaeolithic tool zone dominated by Acheulian handaxes and cleavers, with pebble tools such as choppers and chopping tools occurring alongside them.

notes.name: Bagewadi- Basava
notes.note: Basavana Bagewadi, Vijayapura district, northern Karnataka. C. 1105-1167 CE. The origin of the most thoroughgoing social critique produced by any Indian devotional movement. Basavanna rejected caste, image worship, temple ritual, pilgrimage and the authority of the Vedas.

notes.name: Bagh Caves
notes.note: Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh. Nine rock-cut Buddhist caves of the late Gupta period. The best evidence outside Ajanta for Gupta-age mural painting, and the surviving link in the chain west to Gujarat.

notes.name: Baghor MP
notes.note: II and III, Sidhi district, Madhya Pradesh. Upper Palaeolithic, the shrine dated to about 9000-8000 BCE. Baghor I has yielded the clearest evidence of an Upper Palaeolithic shrine anywhere in the subcontinent, and so of organised religious activity among hunter-gatherers.

notes.name: Bagor
notes.note: Bhilwara district, Rajasthan, on a sand dune beside the Kothari river. Three phases excavated by V. N. Misra. The richest microlithic assemblage in India, and the best evidence that Mesolithic communities kept domesticated animals long before they farmed.

notes.name: Bagram
notes.note: Begram, Parwan province, Afghanistan. The sealed Begram hoard was found in 1937 and 1939 in two walled-up rooms of the palace and dates to the 1st-2nd centuries CE. The richest single assemblage of long-distance trade goods from the ancient world, the Silk Road as an object rather than an argument.

notes.name: Bahapur
notes.note: Near Kalkaji in south Delhi, on a rocky outcrop of the Delhi ridge. C. 258-257 BCE. Extends the Minor Rock Edict distribution into the Delhi region, and confirms the rule that these edicts follow trade roads.

notes.name: Bahawalpur
notes.note: The Bahawalpur region of Punjab (Pakistan). C. 1100-500/400 BCE. Fixes the western extent of PGW and supplies one of the three regional settlement studies on which PGW social history rests.

notes.name: Bairat
notes.note: Jaipur district, Rajasthan. C. 258-257 BCE. The Bhabru edict is the only Ashokan inscription that cites Buddhist scripture by name, the strongest evidence for his personal Buddhism. Opens with Ashoka's salutation and his declaration of reverence and faith in the Buddha.

notes.name: Balaghat or Mahurjhari
notes.note: Mahurjhari lies about 15 km north-west of Nagpur on the Vidarbha uplands. C. 800-400 BCE on the calibrated dates for the group (Naikund gives 800-420 BCE). The richest stone-circle cemetery of Vidarbha and the bead-making capital of the megalithic Deccan.

notes.name: Balakot
notes.note: Las Bela district, Baluchistan. Period I is a pre/early Harappan horizon of the 4th millennium BCE with Nal-related pottery. The best-excavated Harappan coastal village and, with Chanhudaro, one of the two principal shell-working centres of the civilisation.

notes.name: Balathal
notes.note: Udaipur district, Rajasthan, in the Banas-Berach river system, excavated between 1994 and 1998. An Ahar (Banas) culture site of about 2 hectares. Balathal is the Chalcolithic site that overturned the assumption that fortification and planned building were Harappan monopolies.

notes.name: Balkh or Bactria
notes.note: Ancient Bactra. An Achaemenid satrapal seat. The single most important crossroads on the northern route, the place where Greek, Iranian, Indian and Chinese worlds met. The Greco-Bactrian kings, Diodotus, Euthydemus and Demetrius among them.

notes.name: Balu
notes.note: Kaithal district, Haryana, on the Ghaggar-Hakra (Sarasvati) tract of the Indo-Gangetic divide. A small fortified rural settlement with early Harappan levels of the Kalibangan I type (c. 2900-2600 BCE) and a mature Harappan phase (c. 2600-1900 BCE). Yields the fullest archaeobotanical record of any early and mature Harappan site.

notes.name: Bamyan Caves
notes.note: The Bamiyan valley in the Hazarajat of central Afghanistan. A monastic complex of the 3rd-8th centuries CE under Kushana and Hephthalite patronage. The largest standing Buddha images ever carved, and the meeting point of Gandharan, Sasanian and Gupta form.

notes.name: Banahalli
notes.note: In the granite uplands of eastern Karnataka (the Kolar-Chikkaballapur tract). A neolithic-chalcolithic settlement whose upper levels merge into a megalithic phase. Shows the neolithic-to-megalithic continuum of the Karnataka plateau in a single section, where the earliest iron of the region appears in the overlap.

notes.name: Banavasi
notes.note: Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka. A centre under the Satavahanas and the Chutus. The capital of the first indigenous dynasty of the Kannada country, the point at which Karnataka acquires a political history of its own.

notes.name: Banawali
notes.note: Fatehabad district, Haryana. Period I early Harappan (c. 2900-2600 BCE). A fortified town whose plan departs from the standard citadel-and-lower-town formula, and one of the richest sites for reading Harappan social difference.

notes.name: Bangarh
notes.note: Near Gangarampur in Dakshin Dinajpur district, West Bengal. A long sequence whose lowest levels carry a pre-urban Chalcolithic occupation. The principal excavated urban site of northern Bengal, and the main evidence that the Gangetic urban tradition extended east of Bihar.

notes.name: Banimilia Banhera
notes.note: On the northern fringe of the Vindhyas in the Varanasi-Chandauli tract of south-eastern Uttar Pradesh. Part of the south-eastern Uttar Pradesh megalithic province. Belongs to the one Indian megalithic zone that is substantially pre-iron, the standing exception to the equation of megaliths with the iron age.

notes.name: Bannur-Vyastirtha
notes.note: Mysuru district, Karnataka, on the Kaveri in the southern Deccan. Vyasatirtha, or Vyasaraja, 1460-1539. The philosopher-minister of Vijayanagara at its height, and the link between Dvaita philosophy and the Haridasa devotional movement.

notes.name: Barabar Caves
notes.note: The Barabar and Nagarjuni hills, Jehanabad district, Bihar. Mauryan. The oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India, and the only monuments anywhere built by a state for the Ajivikas. Each cave is cut into hard granite and finished to a mirror polish.

notes.name: Barbarium
notes.note: The port at the mouth of the Indus in Sindh, Pakistan. Active in the 1st century CE. The one port where the maritime trade of the Indian Ocean and the overland Silk Route demonstrably meet.

notes.name: Bargaon
notes.note: Saharanpur district, western Uttar Pradesh. Late Harappan to Ochre Coloured Pottery, c. 1900-1300 BCE. The type locality for the late Harappan-OCP overlap, and the centre of the densest OCP concentration in the subcontinent.

notes.name: Bargoan
notes.note: Bargaon, Saharanpur district, western Uttar Pradesh. A late Harappan village of c. 1900-1300 BCE. The type locality for the overlap of the late Harappan and Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP) phases, and a marker of the copper-hoard zone.

notes.name: Bekal
notes.note: Kasaragod district, northern Kerala, on a headland jutting into the Arabian Sea. Built about 1650 by Shivappa Nayaka of Keladi. A purely military coastal fort, and evidence of Karnataka powers pressing south into Malabar.

notes.name: Belum Caves
notes.note: Kolimigundla mandal, Nandyal (formerly Kurnool) district, Andhra Pradesh. Used by Jaina and Buddhist monks in the early centuries BCE-CE. The second longest natural cave system in India, at 3,229 m.

notes.name: Bet Dwarka
notes.note: An island off Okha in the Gulf of Kutch, Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat. Late Harappan, with a thermoluminescence date of c. 1570 BCE. One of the very few late Harappan settlements large enough to be called urban.

notes.name: Bhagwanpura
notes.note: Kurukshetra district, Haryana, on the right bank of the Sarasvati (modern Sarsuti). Period IA is late Harappan, c. 1700-1400 BCE. The type site for the overlap of the late Harappan and PGW cultures, the single most-cited evidence on the Harappan-Vedic relationship.

notes.name: Bhaje Caves
notes.note: Bhaja, near Lonavala in Pune district, Maharashtra. Twenty-two caves of c. 2nd-1st centuries BCE. The earliest surviving chaitya hall that still keeps its wooden fittings, the direct transcription of a timber building into rock.

notes.name: Bhandarpur
notes.note: In the lower Narmada basin of eastern Gujarat. Middle to Upper Palaeolithic. The microblade assemblage recovered here belongs to the class of evidence used to trace the dispersal of anatomically modern humans out of Africa into South Asia.

notes.name: Bharatpur or Noh
notes.note: Noh, near Bharatpur in eastern Rajasthan. Period I OCP, Period II BRW, Period III PGW, c. 1000-600 BCE. Carries the full doab sequence, OCP, BRW, PGW, NBPW, into Rajasthan, and is one of the sites where iron appears before PGW.

notes.name: Bharhut
notes.note: Satna district, Madhya Pradesh. A brick stupa of the Mauryan period. The earliest extensive narrative relief sculpture in India, and the only one that labels its own scenes. Jataka and life-of-the-Buddha scenes are carved on the railing medallions in shallow, flat, frontal relief.

notes.name: Bharuch
notes.note: Ancient Barygaza or Bhrigukachchha. An international port from pre-Mauryan times through the Satavahana. The principal western port of ancient India, and the sea end of the two great overland routes.

notes.name: Bhimbetka
notes.note: Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh. An exceptionally long sequence running from the Lower Palaeolithic through the Mesolithic to the historic period. The single most important prehistoric site in India, combining the longest occupation sequence with the richest body of rock art.

notes.name: Bhirrana
notes.note: Fatehabad district, Haryana, on the left bank of the dry Ghaggar (Sarasvati). Period IA Hakra ware, IB early Harappan, IIA early mature Harappan. A key witness to the indigenous, unbroken origins of the Harappan civilisation on the Ghaggar.

notes.name: Bhita
notes.note: On the left bank of the Yamuna about 18 km south-west of Prayagraj. Occupied from about the 5th-4th centuries BCE through the Mauryan. The clearest excavated plan of an ordinary early historic Indian town, not a capital, but a working commercial settlement.

notes.name: Bhitargaon
notes.note: Kanpur Dehat district, Uttar Pradesh, in the Ganga-Yamuna doab south of Kanpur. Gupta period, c. early 5th century CE. The earliest surviving north Indian temple with a shikhara, and the type-site for Gupta brick-and-terracotta building.

notes.name: Bhitari (Ghazipur)
notes.note: Saidpur tehsil, Ghazipur district, Uttar Pradesh. A red sandstone pillar carrying a Sanskrit inscription of Skandagupta in Gupta Brahmi. The record of the two crises that broke the Gupta empire, the Pushyamitra war and the first Huna invasion.

notes.name: Bhojpur
notes.note: Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, on a sandstone spur above the Betwa. Paramara period, r. c. 1010-1055 CE. An unfinished temple that documents how a medieval Indian temple was actually designed and built, evidence no completed building can give.

notes.name: Bhokardan
notes.note: Ancient Bhogavardhana, Jalna district, Maharashtra. A Satavahana-period trade and craft town. A Deccan manufacturing town caught in the act of producing for the Roman trade.

notes.name: Bidar
notes.note: Northern Karnataka. Bahmani capital from c. 1425-32. The finest surviving Persianate architecture of the Deccan sultanates, and a medieval college whose ruin is itself a historical document. The Mahmud Gawan madrasa was a three-storeyed college with lecture halls, a mosque.

notes.name: Bijnor
notes.note: Rajpur Parsu in Bijnor district, western Uttar Pradesh. One of the two sites where Ochre Coloured Pottery was first identified. A type site of the OCP culture, the ware that gives the whole post-Harappan doab its archaeological name.

notes.name: Birbhanpur
notes.note: Barddhaman district, West Bengal. A Mesolithic microlithic site excavated by B. B. Lal in 1957-58. The type-site of the Mesolithic in Bengal, and an unusual case of a non-geometric microlithic industry.

notes.name: Bisauli
notes.note: Budaun district, western Uttar Pradesh, in the Ganga-Ramganga tract of the upper doab. The site at which Ochre Coloured Pottery was first recognised. Joint type site of the OCP culture, and the source of the anthropomorph that defines the copper hoard debate.

notes.name: Bishnupur
notes.note: Bankura district, West Bengal. Capital of the Malla kings. The fullest expression of the Bengal temple, a regional order built in brick, deriving its form from the thatched village hut.

notes.name: Bithoor
notes.note: Bithur, Kanpur district, Uttar Pradesh. The findspot of 1822. The discovery that created the category: every discussion of the copper hoards begins here. The 1822 harpoon was followed by flat celts.

notes.name: bodhgaya
notes.note: Gaya district, Bihar, on the west bank of the Niranjana (Phalgu/Lilajan). Ashoka built the Vajrasana (diamond throne) and a shrine around the bodhi tree in the 3rd century BCE. The place of the enlightenment, the first of the four great pilgrimage sites.

notes.name: Bojjana Konda Caves
notes.note: Sankaram, comprising the twin hills of Bojjannakonda and Lingalakonda. Occupied from about the 3rd century BCE to the 9th century CE. One of the few sites where all three phases of Buddhism, Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana, can be seen on a single hill.

notes.name: Brahmagir, Jatinga rameshwara and Siddapur
notes.note: Three rock sites within a few kilometres of one another at Brahmagiri. C. 258-257 BCE. The southernmost limit of the Mauryan empire on the ground, and the clearest statement of how a Mauryan province was actually run.

notes.name: Brahmagiri
notes.note: Chitradurga district, Karnataka, on a granite hill in the dry southern Deccan. The South Indian Neolithic or Stone Axe Culture, c. 2000 BCE. The excavation that established the chronological framework for the whole of south Indian archaeology.

notes.name: Budihal
notes.note: Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, northern Karnataka. A South Indian Neolithic settlement of roughly the 2nd millennium BCE. The excavation that reinterpreted ashmounds as parts of living settlements, and the best evidence in Indian prehistory for communal food sharing.

notes.name: Bundi
notes.note: The Bundi region of south-eastern Rajasthan. Rock paintings assigned broadly to the Mesolithic and later prehistoric periods. The largest concentration of prehistoric rock art in Rajasthan, the western counterpart to the Vindhyan shelters at Bhimbetka.

notes.name: Burudih
notes.note: Singhbhum district, Jharkhand, on the Chhotanagpur plateau in the Subarnarekha basin. A Neolithic settlement of the eastern Indian tradition. A site that illustrates both the eastern Indian Neolithic and the interpretive problem of shallow, mixed deposits.

notes.name: Burzahom
notes.note: About 16 km from Srinagar, Kashmir, on a karewa, a raised lacustrine terrace. From about 2900 BCE to the early historic era. The most distinctive Neolithic in India, pit dwellings, a great bone industry, and burial practices found nowhere else in the subcontinent.

notes.name: Chak 86
notes.note: Sri Ganganagar district, northern Rajasthan. A Painted Grey Ware findspot of c. 1100-600 BCE in the Ghaggar-Hakra belt. One of the two westernmost points on the standard PGW distribution map.

notes.name: Champaner
notes.note: Panchmahal district, Gujarat. A Chauhan Rajput stronghold under the Khichi rulers of Pavagadh until Mahmud Begada took it in 1484 after a twenty-month siege. The only complete pre-Mughal Islamic city in India that was never built over, and the best surviving statement of the Gujarat Sultanate style.

notes.name: Champapur
notes.note: Near Bhagalpur, Bihar, where the Champa river joins the Ganga. NBPW c. 600-200 BCE, the phase of the rampart and moat. The fortified nagara of the Buddhist texts, and the first mahajanapada to be swallowed by Magadha.

notes.name: Champaran-Vallabhacharya
notes.note: Also called Champajhar, in Raipur district, Chhattisgarh. Taught during the Lodi and early Mughal period. The founder of the Pushtimarg, the most organised of the Krishna devotional sects, and of the Shuddhadvaita philosophy.

notes.name: Chandragiri Hill
notes.note: The smaller of the two hills at Shravanabelagola, Hassan district, Karnataka. From about the 6th century CE to modern times, Hoysala and Vijayanagara. The largest single body of Jaina inscriptions in India, and the epigraphic basis for the Digambara account of the great schism.

notes.name: Chandraketugarh
notes.note: Berachampa, North 24 Parganas, West Bengal, on the Bidyadhari, a former Ganga distributary. NBPW c. 400-200 BCE, Mauryan. The finest terracotta corpus of early historic India, and the delta's inland answer to the port of Tamralipti.

notes.name: Chanhudaro
notes.note: Sindh. Mature Harappan c. 2500-1900 BCE (5-10 ha). The Harappan industrial town, an unfortified craft settlement rather than a city, and the best single index of Harappan manufacturing. No citadel and no fortification wall, streets with drains covered by burnt brick.

notes.name: Charsada
notes.note: Ancient Pushkalavati. Occupied from about the 6th century BCE. The type-site for the north-west's long exposure to successive foreign powers, and the stratigraphy against which that sequence is dated. Gandhara was the twentieth satrapy of the Achaemenid empire.

notes.name: Chausa
notes.note: Buxar (formerly Bhojpur) district, Bihar. Spanning roughly the 2nd to the 6th centuries CE. The earliest group of Jaina metal images in India, and the eastern counterpart to Akota. Eighteen bronzes: Tirthankaras, yakshis, a makara and a kalpavriksha.

notes.name: Chirand
notes.note: Saran district, Bihar. Running from the Neolithic of about 2500-1500 BCE through Chalcolithic. The type-site of the middle Ganga Neolithic, and the possessor of a bone industry rivalled only by Burzahom.

notes.name: Chitorgarh
notes.note: Chittorgarh, southern Rajasthan. The Sisodia capital of Mewar until 1568. The central symbol of Rajput resistance, and the site of the three jauhars around which that tradition is built. The 1303 siege is the subject of Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Padmavat, written in Awadhi in 1540.

notes.name: Chittagong
notes.note: Chattogram, on the Karnaphuli river near its mouth on the Bay of Bengal. A port from the early medieval period. The Bay of Bengal's principal eastern port, and the frontier where Mughal authority finally met the sea.

notes.name: Chittoor
notes.note: Southern Andhra Pradesh. Middle and Upper Palaeolithic, with continuity of occupation into the Megalithic period. The area shows an unusually complete cultural sequence from the Palaeolithic to the Megalithic. Acheulian tools occur together with Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic material, two sites have been identified.

notes.name: Chopani Mando
notes.note: In the Belan valley on the Vindhyan fringe of the Allahabad (Prayagraj) and Mirzapur tract. A habitation site with a cultural sequence running from the Upper Palaeolithic (Period I) through the Mesolithic (Periods II and III, with geometric microliths in Period IIB) to the Neolithic.

notes.name: Cooch Behar
notes.note: Northern West Bengal. The Koch kingdom was founded by Biswa Singha in the early 16th century and reached its height under Nara Narayan. The seat of the Koch dynasty, and a textbook example of princely-state architecture built to advertise loyalty to the Raj.

notes.name: Dah Parvatiya
notes.note: Da-Parbatia, on the western edge of Tezpur, Sonitpur district, Assam. A carved stone doorframe of the 6th century CE, Gupta idiom. The oldest surviving architectural sculpture in Assam, and the proof that the Gupta classical idiom reached the Brahmaputra valley.

notes.name: Daimabad
notes.note: On the left bank of the Pravara, a tributary of the Godavari. A late Harappan phase (Period II). The largest Chalcolithic settlement of the Deccan, which with Inamgaon shows Jorwe society approaching an urban threshold.

notes.name: Dambulla Cave temple
notes.note: Rangiri Dambulla, Matale district, central Sri Lanka. The caves were monastic shelters with drip-ledges and Brahmi inscriptions from the 3rd-2nd centuries BCE. The largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka, and a continuous record of Theravada image-making over two millennia.

notes.name: Damdana
notes.note: Damdama, Pratapgarh district, Uttar Pradesh. Radiocarbon dates cluster around the 8th-7th millennia BCE. The largest Mesolithic cemetery in India, and the site with the best evidence for plant food processing.

notes.name: Daojali Hading
notes.note: Dima Hasao district, the former North Cachar Hills, of Assam. A Neolithic settlement generally placed around 2700-2000 BCE. The site that placed the north-east in a Southeast Asian rather than an Indian cultural province.

notes.name: Darasuram
notes.note: Near Kumbakonam, Thanjavur district, Tamil Nadu, in the heart of the Kaveri delta. R. c. 1146-1173 CE, in the late Chola period. The last of the three Great Living Chola Temples, and the point at which Chola architecture turns from scale to refinement.

notes.name: Dari Dungari
notes.note: Sambalpur district, Odisha, in the Mahanadi basin. Lower and Middle Palaeolithic. Explorations here recovered a large number of Lower and Middle Palaeolithic tools, making it one of the richest surface concentrations in the Mahanadi system.

notes.name: Debal
notes.note: At the mouth of the Indus in Sindh, Pakistan. Founded in the early centuries CE and prominent through the 7th-13th. The port at which the Arab conquest of Sindh began, and the site of the earliest dated mosque in the subcontinent.

notes.name: Dehu-Tukaram
notes.note: Pune district, Maharashtra, on the Indrayani river about 30 km from Pune. Tukaram, c. 1608-1650, a grain trader of the Kunbi caste. The peak of Marathi devotional poetry, and the sharpest voice against ritual and caste privilege in the tradition.

notes.name: Delhi
notes.note: Two Ashokan pillars in Delhi: the Delhi-Topra pillar at Firoz Shah Kotla. Polished Chunar sandstone shafts of c. 243-242 BCE carrying Pillar Edicts in Brahmi and Prakrit. Topra is the only pillar in India to carry Pillar Edict VII, Ashoka's own review of his reign.

notes.name: Deogarh or Lalitpur Dashavtar
notes.note: Lalitpur district, Uttar Pradesh, on a spur of the Vindhyas above the Betwa. Gupta period, c. 500-525 CE. The classic Gupta temple: the first to combine a shikhara, a sculpted programme and the panchayatana plan.

notes.name: Desalpur
notes.note: Nakhatrana taluka, Kutch district, Gujarat. A mature Harappan fortified settlement of c. 2500-1900 BCE with no early Harappan level (like Lothal, Chanhudaro, Mitathal, Alamgirpur and Ropar). A small fortified Harappan station holding the interior Kutch route, with unusually clear administrative evidence for its size.

notes.name: Dhanesar
notes.note: Banda district, Uttar Pradesh. Bronze images of the Gupta and post-Gupta period, c. 5th-6th centuries CE. An inscribed Gupta bronze that doubles as a historical document for a region with no dynastic record of its own.

notes.name: Dhar
notes.note: Madhya Pradesh, on the Malwa plateau south-west of Indore. Capital of the Paramaras from the 9th century, r. c. 1010-1055 CE. The court of the scholar-king Bhoja, and the site of a documented medieval college.

notes.name: Dharashiv caves
notes.note: The Dharashiv caves, about 8 km from Dharashiv town, formerly Osmanabad. Seven caves excavated between roughly the 5th and 7th centuries CE. A rock-cut group whose conversion from Buddhist to Jaina use is legible in the excavation itself.

notes.name: Didwana or Nagaur
notes.note: Nagaur district, western Rajasthan. A stratigraphic profile extending from the early to the middle Palaeolithic. One of the very few Indian sites with absolute dates for both the Lower and Middle Palaeolithic.

notes.name: Dilwara
notes.note: On Mount Abu, Sirohi district, Rajasthan, the highest point of the Aravallis. Five Jain temples in white Makrana marble built between the 11th and 13th centuries under the Chaulukya (Solanki) kings of Gujarat. The finest marble carving in India.

notes.name: Dwarka
notes.note: Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat. Occupation from the late Harappan and post-Harappan centuries. One of the Char Dham and the Sapta Puri, a working port, and the most contested piece of marine archaeology in India.

notes.name: Edakkal
notes.note: On Ambukuthi hill near Ambalavayal, Wayanad district, Kerala. The earlier assigned to the Neolithic, roughly the 4th-3rd millennia BCE. The only substantial prehistoric petroglyph site in south India, and one of very few anywhere carved rather than painted.

notes.name: Elephanta Caves
notes.note: Gharapuri island in Mumbai harbour, Raigad district, Maharashtra. Mid-6th century CE. The summit of Shaiva rock-cut sculpture in India, a cave conceived as a single theological argument in stone. The Great Cave, about 39 m across, is planned on two axes at once.

notes.name: Ellora or Kailasa
notes.note: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) district, Maharashtra. Thirty-four excavations spanning c. 600-1000 CE: Caves 1-12 Buddhist (6th-8th centuries). The largest monolithic excavation in the world, and the clearest single demonstration of three religions patronised at one site.

notes.name: Eran
notes.note: Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, on the Bina river, a tributary of the Betwa. Period I, roughly 1800-700 BCE. Eran combines an early fortified Chalcolithic village with one of the most important epigraphic sequences of the Gupta age.

notes.name: Etawah
notes.note: Saipai, Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, in the lower Ganga-Yamuna doab near the Yamuna. An excavated OCP settlement of the 2nd millennium BCE. The single most important copper hoard site, because here alone the objects came out of a dated.

notes.name: Fatehpur Sikri
notes.note: Agra district, Uttar Pradesh. Built by Akbar between 1571 and 1585 and occupied as the imperial capital for roughly fourteen years. A complete Mughal capital frozen at one moment, and the setting of Akbar's religious experiment.

notes.name: Fort St George
notes.note: On the Coromandel shore at Chennai, Tamil Nadu. The Nayak governing for the Vijayanagara successor at Chandragiri. The first English fortress in India, and the model for how a trading company turned into a territorial power.

notes.name: Fort St William
notes.note: Fort William, Kolkata, West Bengal. The old fort was built from 1696 to 1706 around the Company's factory at Sutanuti-Kalikata-Govindpur. The base from which the Company conquered Bengal, and therefore India.

notes.name: Gagron Fort
notes.note: Jhalawar district, south-eastern Rajasthan. Built by the Doda and later Khichi Rajputs from about the 12th century. The classic Indian jaldurg or water fort, and a frontier stronghold between Rajasthan and Malwa.

notes.name: Ganeriwala
notes.note: Ganweriwala, in the Cholistan desert of Bahawalpur district, Punjab (Pakistan). Mature Harappan, c. 2600-1900 BCE. One of the five largest Harappan cities and the largest gap in the evidence, an unexcavated capital-scale site.

notes.name: Ganeshwar
notes.note: Near Nim-ka-Thana in Sikar district, north-eastern Rajasthan, on the Kantli-Sahibi drainage. Type site, with Jodhpura, of the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture. A small site of only 1.2 to 1.6 hectares that yielded hundreds of copper objects.

notes.name: Gangaikonda Cholapuram
notes.note: Ariyalur district, Tamil Nadu, north of the Kollidam (Coleroon) in the Kaveri delta. Founded by Rajendra I c. 1025 CE after his northern campaign. A capital founded as a war memorial, the Chola empire at its widest, commemorated in stone and water.

notes.name: Garhgaon
notes.note: Sivasagar district, upper Assam, in the Dikhow valley south of the Brahmaputra. Built as the Ahom capital in 1540 by Suklenmung. The Ahom capital through the century of Mughal invasion, and the base of the resistance that stopped Mughal expansion eastward.

notes.name: Gauda
notes.note: Later Lakhnauti and Gaur, Malda district, West Bengal. Capital of Shashanka's Gauda kingdom in the early 7th century CE. One site carrying a thousand years of Bengal's history, the only recorded election of a king in early India.

notes.name: Ghantasala
notes.note: Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh. A Satavahana and Ikshvaku Buddhist centre, c. 2nd century BCE-3rd century CE. A stupa of unique plan, and the clearest link between Andhra Buddhism and the maritime trade that paid for it.

notes.name: Ghazni
notes.note: Eastern Afghanistan. Capital of the Ghaznavid dynasty. The base from which the Ghaznavid raids on India were mounted, and an unexpected centre of scholarship funded by their proceeds. Mahmud's raids, Nagarkot, Mathura, Kannauj, Somnath in 1025-26, were expeditions for plunder rather than for territory.

notes.name: Gilund
notes.note: Rajsamand district, Rajasthan, in the Banas valley, about 10.5 hectares in extent. Broadly 2100-1500 BCE. Gilund is the Banas culture site that has produced the most substantial architecture. The structural remains include a large mud-brick complex measuring about 30.48 by 24.38 m.

notes.name: Gingee
notes.note: Villupuram district, Tamil Nadu, where three granite hills, Rajagiri, Krishnagiri and Chandrayandurg. Begun under the Konar chiefs and the Cholas. The strongest fortress in the Deccan, and the base from which the Maratha state survived Aurangzeb's conquest of Maharashtra.

notes.name: Girnar or Jungadh
notes.note: A granite boulder beside the road from Junagadh to the Girnar hills, Gujarat. C. 257-256 BCE. The only surface in India carrying Mauryan, Shaka-Kshatrapa and Gupta records together, seven centuries of imperial history on one stone.

notes.name: Golbai Sasan
notes.note: Khordha district, Odisha. Three periods excavated by the Odisha state archaeology department: Period I Neolithic from about 2300 BCE. The reference sequence for coastal Odisha, and one of the few Indian sites where Neolithic.

notes.name: Golconda
notes.note: On a granite hill on the western edge of Hyderabad, Telangana. A Kakatiya mud fort rebuilt in stone by the Qutb Shahis from 1518. The diamond capital of the world, and the conquest that completed Aurangzeb's overextension in the Deccan.

notes.name: Gudiyam Caves
notes.note: In the hills of the Kortallayar basin, Tiruvallur district, not far from Chennai. Middle and Upper Palaeolithic tools. The cave has yielded a complete Lower-to-Upper Palaeolithic tool sequence, one of the few cave stratigraphies available in South India.

notes.name: Gufkral
notes.note: Pulwama district, Kashmir. Period IA is aceramic Neolithic, IB and IC ceramic Neolithic. The Kashmir Neolithic with an aceramic phase, farming before pottery, as at Mehrgarh, which makes it the more informative of the two Kashmir sites.

notes.name: Gujjara
notes.note: Gujarra, Datia district, Madhya Pradesh, in the Bundelkhand uplands. C. 258-257 BCE. One of the handful of inscriptions that give Ashoka's personal name, without which the edicts would belong to an anonymous "Devanampiya Piyadasi".

notes.name: Gulbarga
notes.note: Kalaburagi, formerly Gulbarga, northern Karnataka. Capital of the Bahmani sultanate from 1347. The first capital of the first independent Deccan sultanate, and the place where the Chishti order moved south.

notes.name: Gumarwin
notes.note: Ghumarwin, Bilaspur district, Himachal Pradesh, in the Siwalik foothills of the Sutlej basin. Lower Palaeolithic. The association of Acheulian and Soanian tools at one locality argues against treating the two as separate and mutually exclusive cultures.

notes.name: Gumla
notes.note: Dera Ismail Khan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Six periods excavated by A. H. Dani. A long sequence on one of the main routes between Central Asia and the Indus. Period II has pit dwellings and hand-made pottery, Period III-IV bring mud-brick architecture.

notes.name: Gungeria
notes.note: Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh, in the Satpura uplands of the upper Wainganga basin. Chalcolithic. Gungeria produced the largest copper hoard ever found in India: 424 copper tools and weapons together with 102 thin sheets of silver objects.

notes.name: Gwalior
notes.note: Madhya Pradesh. Occupied from at least the 6th century CE. The home of the earliest known written zero, and of the finest pre-Mughal Hindu palace architecture in northern India.

notes.name: Gyaraspur
notes.note: Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh. Pratihara period, 9th-10th centuries CE. A compact set of Pratihara-period monuments that fills the gap between Gupta Malwa and Chandela Bundelkhand. The Maladevi temple is built against a hillside, half rock-cut and half structural.

notes.name: Halebeedu
notes.note: Halebidu, ancient Dorasamudra, Hassan district, Karnataka. Hoysala capital from the 11th century to 1327. The peak of Hoysala architecture, a distinct Deccan order that is neither Nagara nor Dravida. The plan is stellate: a star-shaped sanctum and outer wall on a raised jagati platform that follows the same profile.

notes.name: Hallur
notes.note: Haveri district, Karnataka. Period I is Neolithic-Chalcolithic, from about 2000 BCE. One of the earliest dates for iron in peninsular India, and the site that established millet farming in the southern Neolithic.

notes.name: Halmidi
notes.note: Belur taluk, Hassan district, Karnataka. A stone pillar inscription of c. 450-500 CE. The earliest full-length inscription in the Kannada language, the point at which Kannada becomes a written language.

notes.name: Hampi
notes.note: Vijayanagara district, Karnataka. Capital of the Vijayanagara empire from its founding in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka to its sack in 1565 after the battle of Talikota. The largest medieval Hindu capital to survive as a ruin, and the type-site of the Vijayanagara architectural order.

notes.name: Harappa
notes.note: Sahiwal district, Punjab (Pakistan), on an old bed of the Ravi. Period I Ravi/Hakra phase, Period II early Harappan, Period III mature Harappan. The type site that names the civilisation, and the only city with a documented sequence from the Ravi phase to the late Harappan.

notes.name: Hastinapur
notes.note: Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh. Period I OCP, Period II PGW, c. 1100-800 BCE, Period III NBPW. The excavation that established what PGW meant, and the classic attempt to tie Indian archaeology to the Mahabharata.

notes.name: Hathigumpha
notes.note: The Hathigumpha, or Elephant Cave. Generally assigned to the 1st century BCE. The fullest royal autobiography from ancient India, a year-by-year account of a reign, with no parallel in the period.

notes.name: Hathnora
notes.note: On the northern bank of the Narmada about 40 km north-east of Hoshangabad. In a late Acheulian to Middle Palaeolithic context. The only well-authenticated Pleistocene hominid fossil locality in India, which places the subcontinent within the global story of human evolution.

notes.name: Hawa Mahal
notes.note: The Hawa Mahal, in the walled city of Jaipur, Rajasthan. Built in 1799 by Sawai Pratap Singh, designed by Lal Chand Ustad. Purdah made architectural, a building whose entire design exists to let women see without being seen.

notes.name: Hemis gompa Monastery
notes.note: Leh district, Ladakh. A monastery existed on the site before the 11th century. The wealthiest and largest monastery in Ladakh, and the standard example of royal patronage creating a monastic order's dominance.

notes.name: Herat
notes.note: Western Afghanistan, on the Hari Rud in the province of Khurasan. An ancient city, sacked by the Mongols in 1221. The Timurid capital whose artistic tradition the Mughals brought to India, the aesthetic ancestor of Mughal painting.

notes.name: Hiran Valley
notes.note: The Hiran river valley in Saurashtra, Gujarat. Lower Palaeolithic dated between 190,000 and 69,000 BP. One of the very few sequences in Gujarat to carry absolute dates for both the Lower and the Middle Palaeolithic.

notes.name: Hunasgi
notes.note: The Hunsgi valley, Gulbarga (Kalaburagi) district, Karnataka, on the banks of the Hunsgi. Lower Palaeolithic (Acheulian). The classic Indian demonstration of Acheulian settlement patterns. Sites with very few artefact types represent places where specific activities such as tool-making or killing game were carried out.

notes.name: Imlidih
notes.note: On the banks of the Kuwana river in Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh. Period I represents the pre-Narhan culture and goes back to about 1300 BCE.

notes.name: Inamgaon
notes.note: On the Ghod river, a tributary of the Bhima, in Pune district, Maharashtra. A Chalcolithic sequence covering the Malwa and Jorwe phases. The most completely excavated Chalcolithic village in India, and the site on which almost all reconstructions of Chalcolithic social organisation.

notes.name: Indraprastha
notes.note: The Purana Qila mound, Delhi, on the old west bank of the Yamuna. C. 1000 BCE, NBPW from c. 300 BCE, Gupta. One of the few north Indian mounds with an unbroken PGW-to-Mughal sequence, and the archaeological anchor for the Pandava capital.

notes.name: Jagaddala
notes.note: Dhamoirhat upazila, Naogaon district, north-west Bangladesh, in Varendra. C. 1077-1120 CE, flourishing into the early 13th century. The last of the five great Pala mahaviharas to rise, and the bridge by which Vajrayana learning passed to Tibet.

notes.name: Jagannath and Konark Sun Temple
notes.note: Puri and Konark, on the Odisha coast of the Bay of Bengal. The Jagannath temple at Puri was begun by Anantavarman Chodaganga c. 1135 CE and completed under Anangabhima III. The culmination of Odishan architecture, and the state cult on which Ganga and Gajapati kingship rested.

notes.name: Jaipur
notes.note: The Jaipur district of north-eastern Rajasthan. Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture. Jodhpura and the Jaipur district sites represent the eastern wing of the copper-working complex that supplied metal to the early and mature Harappans.

notes.name: Jaisalmer
notes.note: Western Rajasthan. Founded in 1156 CE by Rawal Jaisal of the Bhati Rajputs. A desert caravan city, one of the very few forts anywhere still inhabited as a town. Jaisalmer's wealth came entirely from transit.

notes.name: Jalna-Ramdas
notes.note: Jamb near Jalna, Maharashtra, in the Godavari basin of Marathwada, is Ramdas's birthplace. Samarth Ramdas, 1608-1681. The saint of activist devotion, the counter-model to the Varkari tradition, and the figure invoked to give Maratha power a religious sanction.

notes.name: Jaugada
notes.note: Ganjam district, Odisha. C. 257-256 BCE. One of only two sites, with Dhauli, where Ashoka replaced the standard edicts with a text written specially for a conquered people. Rock Edicts 11, 12 and 13 are omitted here and at Dhauli.

notes.name: Jhukar Late Harappa
notes.note: Larkana district, Sindh, on the Indus plain a short distance from Mohenjodaro. The late Harappan phase of Sindh, c. 1900-1500 BCE. Gives Sindh its post-urban identity and shows that the transition from the mature phase was gradual, not a rupture.

notes.name: Jorve
notes.note: Jorwe, on the left bank of the Pravara river. Dated about 1400-700 BCE. Jorwe gives its name to the most widespread Chalcolithic culture of the Deccan, known from roughly 200 sites.

notes.name: Junagadh Caves
notes.note: Gujarat, at the foot of the Girnar hills in Saurashtra. Mauryan, c. 3rd century BCE. The caves are Gujarat's Buddhist record. The Girnar rock holds Ashoka's fourteen Major Rock Edicts.

notes.name: Junapani
notes.note: About 10 km north-west of Nagpur in Vidarbha, Maharashtra. Among the earliest megaliths ever recorded in India. The type site of the Vidarbha stone-circle burial and the principal Indian site for cup-marked megalithic stones.

notes.name: Junnar Caves
notes.note: Pune district, Maharashtra, on the Kukadi river below the Naneghat pass. Cut between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE. The largest concentration of rock-cut caves in India, and the clearest case of Buddhist establishments following a trade route rather than a capital.

notes.name: Kabul
notes.note: Eastern Afghanistan. A Hindu Shahi centre before the Ghaznavids, taken by Babur in 1504. The Mughal dynasty's own homeland and the empire's strategic hinge, the reason so much Mughal effort went north-west rather than south.

notes.name: Kakoria
notes.note: On the northern fringe of the Vindhyas in south-eastern Uttar Pradesh. Pre-iron megalithic. The best-documented habitation-plus-cemetery pairing in the pre-iron megalithic province of the Vindhyas. The megaliths are cairns and stone circles, some graves show fractional burial.

notes.name: Kaladi-Adi Shakaracharya
notes.note: Kalady, Ernakulam district, Kerala. Usually dated c. 788-820 CE. The birthplace of the philosopher who gave Advaita Vedanta its systematic form and gave Hinduism an institutional structure. Shankara's commentaries on the Brahma Sutras.

notes.name: Kalibangan
notes.note: Hanumangarh district, northern Rajasthan. Period I early Harappan, calibrated c. 2920-2550 BCE, Period II mature Harappan. The third great Harappan city dug in India and the clearest early-to-mature transition anywhere in the culture zone.

notes.name: Kallur4
notes.note: Raichur district, northern Karnataka. A neolithic-megalithic settlement of the Karnataka plateau whose copper hoard is placed in the late 2nd to early 1st millennium BCE. Carries the copper hoard tradition a thousand kilometres south of the doab, and so defines the outer limit of the phenomenon.

notes.name: Kalpi
notes.note: Jalaun district, Uttar Pradesh, on the southern bank of the Yamuna. Middle Palaeolithic. Kalpi preserves the earliest trace of human occupation in the Ganga plain, a region where deep alluvium normally conceals or destroys Palaeolithic evidence.

notes.name: Kalsi
notes.note: Dehradun district, Uttarakhand. C. 257-256 BCE. The northernmost Major Rock Edict site in India, and the one that carries a carved symbol alongside the text. An elephant is carved beside the inscription with the word "gajatame", the supreme elephant.

notes.name: Kalyan
notes.note: Thane district, Maharashtra. Active from the early centuries CE under the Satavahanas and Western Kshatrapas. A port whose classical description records commercial warfare between two Indian dynasties, the sharpest such passage in ancient Indian sources.

notes.name: Kalyani or Basavakalyan
notes.note: Basavakalyan, ancient Kalyani, Bidar district, northern Karnataka. From about 1050 CE under Someshvara I until the dynasty's fall around 1190. The court that produced the standard text of Hindu inheritance law, and the town where the Lingayat movement began.

notes.name: Kamakhya
notes.note: On the Nilachal hill in Guwahati, Assam. Referred to from about the 8th-9th centuries and elaborated under the Palas of Kamarupa. The principal Shakta pitha of eastern India and the chief centre of Tantric worship in the subcontinent.

notes.name: Kambadahalli
notes.note: Mandya district, Karnataka, in the Kaveri basin near Shravanabelagola. Built under the Western Gangas between about the 9th and 10th centuries CE. The finest Ganga-period Jaina temple in Karnataka, and a rare example of the five-shrined panchakuta plan.

notes.name: Kampiliya
notes.note: Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh. Occupation begins in the PGW phase, c. 1100-600 BCE. A Mahajanapada capital whose occupation demonstrably begins in the PGW phase, the archaeological test of the epic and Vedic geography.

notes.name: Kanchipuram
notes.note: Tamil Nadu, on the Vegavathi, a tributary of the Palar. Later the Pallava capital from the 6th to the 9th centuries. One of the seven moksha-puris, and the place where the southern structural stone temple begins.

notes.name: Kandahar
notes.note: Old Kandahar (Shar-i-Kuna), southern Afghanistan. Three groups of texts. The only Ashokan texts in Greek, proof that the empire administered in the languages of its subjects, not only its own.

notes.name: Kanganahalli
notes.note: Near Sannati village, Chitapur taluk, Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, Karnataka. Built c. 3rd century BCE and encased with carved limestone slabs in the Satavahana period. The only known portrait of Ashoka, and a royal gallery of the Satavahana dynasty in stone.

notes.name: Kangla
notes.note: In the centre of Imphal, Manipur. Beginning its record in 33 CE. The centre of Meitei kingship, and the site of one of the last independent kingdoms absorbed into British India.

notes.name: Kanheri Caves
notes.note: In the basalt hills of Salsette island inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park, Mumbai. About 110 caves cut continuously from the 1st century BCE to the 10th century CE. A complete Buddhist university-monastery in rock.

notes.name: Kannauj
notes.note: Ancient Kanyakubja, on the right bank of the Ganga in Kannauj district. A Maukhari capital in the 6th century. The city that stood for paramountcy in northern India, whoever held it claimed to be the successor of Harsha.

notes.name: Kannur
notes.note: The Cannanore of European sources, on the north Malabar coast of Kerala. Prominent in the 12th-15th centuries in trade with Persia and Arabia. The horse port of the Malabar coast, and the seat of Kerala's only Muslim ruling house.

notes.name: Kapilavastu
notes.note: Capital of the Shakya gana, claimed by two sites: Tilaurakot in Kapilvastu district. Tilaurakot, excavated by Debala Mitra (1962) and later Nepali. The Buddha's home for his first twenty-nine years, and the one major Buddhist site whose location is still genuinely in dispute.

notes.name: Karachi
notes.note: Sindh, Pakistan, on the Arabian Sea west of the Indus delta. Identified with the Krokola from which Alexander's admiral Nearchus began his voyage back along the coast in 325 BCE. The maritime gateway of the north-west, where the Indus route meets the sea and the overland Iranian routes meet both.

notes.name: Karaikal - Ammaiyar
notes.note: A coastal enclave of the union territory of Puducherry on the Arasalar. Usually placed in the 6th century CE. One of only three women among the Nayanmars, and the author of the earliest datable Shaiva poetry in Tamil.

notes.name: Karle Caves
notes.note: Karla, near Lonavala in Pune district, Maharashtra. Developed from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE. The largest and most perfectly finished rock-cut chaitya hall in India, the form at its height, just before the Buddha image displaces the stupa.

notes.name: Kaushambi
notes.note: Near Prayagraj in Uttar Pradesh, on the left bank of the Yamuna. The PGW phase is followed by NBPW from c. 600 BCE. The largest PGW settlement of the eastern doab, and the place where the PGW village landscape visibly turns into a city.

notes.name: Kaytha
notes.note: Kayatha, Ujjain district, Madhya Pradesh, on the banks of the Chhoti Kali Sindh. Placed by calibrated radiocarbon dates in the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE and commonly given as about 2000-1800 BCE. Kayatha, with Eran, represents the earliest established Chalcolithic settlement of central India.

notes.name: Kesariya
notes.note: East Champaran district, Bihar, on an old bank of the Gandak (Narayani). A stupa with a possibly Mauryan core. The tallest Buddhist stupa in India, and the closest Indian parallel to the terraced mandala stupas of South-East Asia.

notes.name: Key Gompa Monastery
notes.note: Key (Ki) Gompa, Spiti valley, Lahaul and Spiti district, Himachal Pradesh. Founded c. 1100 CE by Dromton. The largest monastery in Spiti and its principal training centre for lamas, and a building whose form was dictated by warfare.

notes.name: Khajuraho
notes.note: Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh, in Bundelkhand between the Ken and the Betwa, Jejakabhukti. Chandela period, c. 900-1050 CE. The high point of the Nagara temple, and the largest concentrated act of temple patronage by any early medieval dynasty.

notes.name: Khambat
notes.note: Khambhat, the Cambay of European sources. The dominant port of western India from about the 11th century to the 16th. The Mughal empire's principal outlet to the western Indian Ocean, and a bead industry with four thousand years of continuity.

notes.name: Katarmal Sun Temple
notes.note: Almora district, Uttarakhand. C. 9th century CE. The second most important sun temple in India after Konark, and the principal monument of the Katyuri kingdom. A main shrine of stone in a simplified Nagara idiom stands within a group of about forty-five subsidiary shrines.

notes.name: Kibbanahalli
notes.note: Tumkur district, southern Karnataka, in the upper Cauvery drainage. Middle Palaeolithic. One of the type localities for the Middle Palaeolithic flake industries of southern Karnataka. Finds include handaxes and guillotine chisels.

notes.name: Kili Gul Mohammad
notes.note: In the Quetta valley of Balochistan, Pakistan, below the Bolan pass. The type-site for the Quetta valley sequence. The ceramic sequence by which the Baluchistan Chalcolithic is dated, the chronological framework for everything preceding the Harappans in the north-west.

notes.name: Kodihwa
notes.note: Koldihwa, Allahabad (Prayagraj) district, Uttar Pradesh. A sequence showing cultural continuity from the Neolithic through the Chalcolithic to the Iron Age. Koldihwa is at the centre of the debate on the origins of rice cultivation in India.

notes.name: Kodungallur or Mahodayapuram
notes.note: The Cranganore of European sources, Thrissur district, Kerala. Capital of the Chera Perumals from about the 9th century to the early 12th. The Chera Perumal capital, and the single stretch of Indian coast where Judaism, Christianity and Islam each claim their first foothold.

notes.name: Kolar
notes.note: Karnataka. An early capital of the Western Gangas before they moved to Talakad. India's principal gold field, worked from antiquity, and an early Ganga seat. The Kolar Gold Fields were mined long before the shafts of the colonial period.

notes.name: Kollam
notes.note: The Quilon of European sources. Refounded in 825 CE. The port that produced the finest surviving document of multi-religious commerce in early medieval India. The Tharisapalli copper plates of c. 849 CE, issued by Ayyanadikal Thiruvadikal of Venad.

notes.name: Kondana Caves
notes.note: Near Karjat in Raigad district, Maharashtra. A group of sixteen Buddhist excavations of the Hinayana phase. One of the earliest western Deccan cave groups, and an unusually clear case of stone imitating carpentry.

notes.name: Korkai
notes.note: Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu, on the Thamirabarani river near the Gulf of Mannar. Flourishing c. 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE. The centre of the ancient pearl fishery, a port built on one commodity, and the Pandya kingdom's origin.

notes.name: Kot Diji
notes.note: Khairpur district, Sindh. Early Harappan Period I dated from c. 3300 BCE. Type site of the 'Kot Dijian' horizon, the widest early Harappan cultural umbrella, from Cholistan to the Gomal and the Potwar.

notes.name: Kotia
notes.note: In the Belan valley of south-eastern Uttar Pradesh (the Prayagraj-Mirzapur tract). Dated c. 800-300 BCE. The exception that carries iron in a largely pre-iron megalithic region, and therefore the site that dates the arrival of iron in the Vindhyas.

notes.name: Kozhikode
notes.note: The Calicut of European and Arabic sources. A Chera-period settlement that became the seat of the Zamorin (Samoothiri) from about the 13th century and the dominant Malabar port through the 14th-16th centuries. The port where the European age in Indian history begins.

notes.name: Kuchai
notes.note: Mayurbhanj district, northern Odisha, near Baripada on the Chhotanagpur plateau fringe. A Mesolithic settlement with a Neolithic phase above it. The site that established Mesolithic-to-Neolithic continuity in eastern India, a transition visible in one stratigraphy rather than inferred.

notes.name: Kuda Caves
notes.note: Near Mandad in Raigad district, Maharashtra. Twenty-six small caves of c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE. Modest caves with first-rate inscriptions, the record of a Konkan feudatory house and of the ordinary people who paid for Buddhist monuments.

notes.name: Kudumiyamalai
notes.note: Pudukkottai district, Tamil Nadu. A musical inscription of about the 7th century CE. The oldest treatise on Indian music surviving anywhere in the world, and a notation, not a description.

notes.name: Kumbhalgarh
notes.note: Rajsamand district, Rajasthan, on a spur of the Aravallis at about 1,100 m. Built by Rana Kumbha of Mewar, r. 1433-1468. The refuge fortress of Mewar, the place the dynasty retreated to when Chittor fell, and the reason it survived.

notes.name: Kumbharia
notes.note: Banaskantha district, northern Gujarat. Five Jaina temples in white marble built under the Chaulukya (Solanki) kings between the 11th and 13th centuries CE. The Solanki marble tradition at its earliest and best, and the immediate context for the more famous temples at Dilwara.

notes.name: Kunal
notes.note: Fatehabad district, Haryana, on the dry Sarasvati-Ghaggar in the Indo-Gangetic divide. Period IA Hakra ware, Period IB early Harappan with Kalibangan I pottery. Documents both the architectural shift from pit dwellings to a planned brick village and the earliest concentration of elite wealth in the Harappan tradition.

notes.name: Kunjhun
notes.note: In the Son valley of Sidhi district, Madhya Pradesh. A prehistoric locality in the Son valley sequence. Part of the Son valley sequence, one of the few places in India where Palaeolithic.

notes.name: Kuntasi
notes.note: Morbi district, Gujarat. Harappan. A specialised Harappan manufacturing and shipping outpost, evidence that the civilisation's coastal network included small industrial stations, not only cities. The settlement is dominated by workshops rather than housing: bead-making debris in carnelian, agate and steatite.

notes.name: Kuntitoli
notes.note: On the Chotanagpur plateau of Jharkhand. Burials of the 1st millennium BCE in a region where megalith building survived as a living practice among the Munda-speaking peoples into modern times. Represents the eastern Indian megalithic province, where archaeology and ethnography can be read together.

notes.name: Kupgal
notes.note: Near Sanganakallu on the granite hills outside Ballari, Karnataka. South Indian Neolithic with a Chalcolithic overlap, roughly 3000-1200 BCE. A Neolithic ritual landscape, the clearest Indian evidence that prehistoric sites were used for ceremony as well as habitation.

notes.name: Kurki - Mirabai
notes.note: Kudki, or Kurki, in Pali district, Rajasthan. Mirabai, c. 1498-1547, was a Rathore princess of Merta married to Bhojraj. The best-known woman in the north Indian bhakti tradition, and a case of devotion used to refuse the obligations of rank and marriage.

notes.name: Kurnool
notes.note: The Kurnool cave complex, including Muchchatla Chintamanu Gavi and the Billa Surgam caves. Upper Palaeolithic. Kurnool and Muchchatla Chintamanu Gavi are the only places in the subcontinent where tools made of animal bone have been found in an Upper Palaeolithic context.

notes.name: Kushinagar
notes.note: Kasia, Kushinagar district, Uttar Pradesh, on the Hiranyavati (the Little Gandak). Identified by Cunningham and excavated by A. C. L. Carlleyle in 1876. The place of the Buddha's Mahaparinirvana, and the capital of one of the two Malla republics.

notes.name: Laghman Minor RE
notes.note: Eastern Afghanistan, on the Alishang and Alingar rivers north of Jalalabad. Aramaic inscriptions of Ashoka's period, c. 260-250 BCE. The furthest north-west that Mauryan authority is attested in writing, and the only Ashokan texts that read like road markers.

notes.name: Lahore
notes.note: Punjab, Pakistan, on the left bank of the Ravi in the Bari doab. The Ghaznavids' Indian capital from the 11th century after Mahmud's raids. The Mughal empire's second capital, and the best place to see Mughal garden and mosque architecture at full scale.

notes.name: Lahrudeva
notes.note: Lahuradewa, Sant Kabir Nagar district, eastern Uttar Pradesh. Period IA yielded pottery and rice from the 7th millennium BCE. The strongest current claim for very early rice in India, and the site that reopened the question of an independent Gangetic agricultural origin.

notes.name: Lakhudiyar
notes.note: On the bank of the Suyal river about 20 km from Almora on the Almora-Barechhina road. Rock paintings assigned broadly to the Mesolithic and later prehistoric periods. The principal prehistoric rock art site of the central Himalaya, the northern counterpart to Bhimbetka.

notes.name: Lal Ded - Pandrethan
notes.note: Pandrethan, ancient Puranadhisthana, on the outskirts of Srinagar beside the Jhelum. A generation into the Shah Mir sultanate and contemporary with the arrival of Sayyid Ali Hamadani and the spread of Islam in the valley. The founding voice of Kashmiri literature, and a figure claimed by both Hindus and Muslims.

notes.name: Lalitgiri
notes.note: Cuttack district, Odisha, on the Birupa river in the Assia range. Occupied from about the 1st century BCE to the 13th century CE. The rare case of an excavated stupa yielding what are claimed as corporeal relics of the Buddha.

notes.name: Lamayuru Monsatery
notes.note: Leh district, Ladakh. Founded in the 11th century in the period of Rinchen Zangpo. The western Himalayan monastery that best preserves the memory of the "second diffusion" of Buddhism from India into Tibet.

notes.name: Lampaka Minor RE
notes.note: The Sanskrit name for the Laghman region of eastern Afghanistan. Aramaic inscriptions of c. 260-250 BCE. Fixes the north-western administrative frontier of the Maurya empire, in the province the Sanskrit sources call Lampaka.

notes.name: Langhnaj
notes.note: Mehsana district, north Gujarat. Among the earliest scientific excavations of an Indian prehistoric site. The type-site of the Gujarat Mesolithic. Fourteen human burials were recovered, laid in crouched position.

notes.name: Lauria Nandangarh and Lauriya Araraj
notes.note: Two pillars about 25 km apart in West Champaran district, Bihar. C. 243-242 BCE. The best-preserved Ashokan pillar still standing on its original site, and the model for what a complete pillar looked like.

notes.name: Leh
notes.note: Leh, Ladakh. A settlement of the Ladakh region from early times. The hinge of the trans-Himalayan trade, and the route by which Indian Buddhism reached Tibet and survived there. Leh was the entrepot of the pashmina trade.

notes.name: Lewan
notes.note: In the Bannu basin of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Early Harappan, going back to the early 3rd millennium BCE. The clearest factory site of the Harappan age, an industrial locality rather than a settlement, and proof of specialised production before urbanism.

notes.name: Lhasa
notes.note: In the valley of the Kyi Chu. Made the capital by Srongtsen Gampo in the 7th century CE. The destination of the Indian Buddhist transmission, and the reason much of Indian Buddhist literature survives at all.

notes.name: Lingaraj temple
notes.note: Bhubaneswar, Odisha. Begun under the Somavamshi king Jajati Keshari and completed c. 1090-1104 CE. The mature Kalinga temple, with all four components present for the first time, the standard against which Odishan architecture is described.

notes.name: Lingsugur- Same as Maski 1st palae site to be discovered
notes.note: Raichur district, Karnataka, in the Krishna-Tungabhadra doab, close to Maski. Palaeolithic surface finds. In 1842 Dr Primrose reported stone implements from Lingsugur, the earliest recorded discovery of a prehistoric stone tool in India.

notes.name: Lonar
notes.note: Buldhana district, Maharashtra, in the Deccan trap country of Vidarbha. The crater was formed by a hypervelocity impact in basalt. The only large impact crater in basalt anywhere in the world, and a Puranic site whose myth encodes its own geology.

notes.name: Loteshwar
notes.note: Patan district, north Gujarat, on a sand dune, locally a tekri. Two periods, excavated by P. Ajithprasad of MS University, Baroda. The type-site of the Anarta tradition, and the clearest sequence anywhere in Gujarat from foraging to herding.

notes.name: Lothal
notes.note: In the Bhal tract of Ahmedabad district, Gujarat. Period A is mature Harappan, c. 2400-1900 BCE. The best-planned small Harappan town and the civilisation's principal port on the Gujarat coast.

notes.name: Lumbini
notes.note: Rupandehi district, Nepal. C. 563 BCE by the conventional reckoning. The first of the four great pilgrimage places, and the only Ashokan inscription that records a tax concession.

notes.name: Lumbini Pillar Inscription
notes.note: The pillar standing in the sacred garden at Lumbini, Rupandehi district, Nepal. C. 249 BCE. The only Ashokan inscription that records a specific tax concession, the single most concrete piece of evidence for Mauryan land revenue.

notes.name: Luni Valley
notes.note: The Luni valley of western Rajasthan. Stray finds of Lower Palaeolithic tools, a well-represented Middle Palaeolithic. The valley gives its name to the "Luni industry", the term used for Middle Palaeolithic assemblages west of the Aravallis.

notes.name: Macchilapatnam
notes.note: Machilipatnam, also Masulipatnam or Bandar, Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh. A port from the Satavahana period. The export point for the Coromandel textile trade, the industry that drew European companies to India in the first place.

notes.name: Madurai
notes.note: Tamil Nadu. C. 3rd century BCE onward. One of the very few Indian cities that has been a capital continuously for over two thousand years. Tamil tradition places the third Sangam here under Pandya patronage.

notes.name: Madurai Meenakshi temple
notes.note: Tamil Nadu, on the south bank of the Vaigai, the ancient Pandya capital. A shrine of the Pandya period. The fullest realisation of the Nayaka temple-city, and the rare major temple where the goddess outranks her consort.

notes.name: Mahabalipuram
notes.note: Mamallapuram, Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu. Two Pallava phases. The site where south Indian architecture moves from rock-cut to structural building. The Pancha Rathas are five monolithic shrines cut from single granite boulders.

notes.name: Mahadaha
notes.note: Pratapgarh district, Uttar Pradesh. A Mesolithic lake-side settlement of roughly the 6th-5th millennia BCE. The clearest evidence anywhere in India that a Mesolithic camp was deliberately organised into zones for different activities.

notes.name: Mahagara
notes.note: Prayagraj district, Uttar Pradesh. A Neolithic village excavated by G. R. Sharma of Allahabad University. The clearest direct evidence of cattle penning in the Indian Neolithic, and the centre of the longest-running controversy in Indian prehistory.

notes.name: Mahasthangarh
notes.note: Bogura (Bogra) district, Bangladesh, on the west bank of the Karatoya, ancient Pundranagara. Occupation runs from the 3rd century BCE (Mauryan, with NBPW) to the 18th century CE. The eastern limit of Mauryan administration on the ground, proved by an inscription rather than inferred from a map.

notes.name: Mahishadal
notes.note: Purba Medinipur district, West Bengal. A Chalcolithic settlement dated to roughly 1600-1400 BCE in its earlier phase. One of the small group of sites that define the Bengal Chalcolithic, and a good illustration of how early iron reached eastern India.

notes.name: Malayadipatti
notes.note: Pudukkottai district, Tamil Nadu. Two rock-cut shrines of about the 8th century CE. A rare paired Shaiva and Vaishnava rock-cut group, and one of the few Tamil sites where mural painting survives over sculpture.

notes.name: Malkhed
notes.note: Ancient Manyakheta, Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, Karnataka. Rashtrakuta capital from c. 814 CE. The capital of the dynasty an Arab geographer ranked among the four great kingdoms of the world. Al-Masudi, writing in the 10th century.

notes.name: Malprabha Ghatprabha valley
notes.note: The Malaprabha and Ghataprabha valleys. A stratigraphic sequence of Lower and Upper Palaeolithic tools has been identified in these valleys. One of the few stratified rather than surface Palaeolithic sequences in the Deccan.

notes.name: Manali
notes.note: Kullu district, Himachal Pradesh. Built in 1553 CE by Raja Bahadur Singh of Kullu around an older rock shrine. The best-known example of the Himalayan timber pagoda temple, and a clear case of a local goddess absorbed into the Sanskritic epic.

notes.name: Manda
notes.note: Jammu district. Period I pre-Harappan, Period II mature Harappan, c. 2500-1900 BCE. Fixes the northern frontier of the Harappan world and identifies its timber-procurement zone. Harappan red ware in the full range, jars, dish-on-stand, beakers, goblets and perforated vessels.

notes.name: Mandla
notes.note: Eastern Madhya Pradesh, in the upper Narmada valley below Amarkantak. Palaeolithic surface finds. The locality illustrates the extraordinary geological depth of the upper Narmada, where prehistoric tools occur in a landscape of much older fossil beds.

notes.name: Mandsaur
notes.note: Western Madhya Pradesh, on the Chambal-Malwa plateau. Lower Palaeolithic. At Daraki Chattan more than five hundred pieces of rock art, cup-shaped depressions pecked into the quartzite, have been found together with hammer stones.

notes.name: Mandu
notes.note: Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh, on a Vindhyan plateau about 630 m high. Fortified from the 10th-11th centuries. The finest provincial Sultanate architecture in India, and the building the Taj Mahal's architects came to study.

notes.name: Mansehra
notes.note: Hazara division, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. C. 257-256 BCE. One of only two Ashokan sites written in Kharoshthi, the evidence that Mauryan administration adapted to the script its subjects already used.

notes.name: Martand Sun temple
notes.note: Near Mattan in Anantnag district, Kashmir. R. c. 724-760 CE. The definitive monument of the Kashmiri style, the one regional order in India that absorbs classical Mediterranean form. The plan is a colonnaded quadrangle of eighty-four fluted columns enclosing a central shrine.

notes.name: Maski
notes.note: Raichur district, Karnataka, on the Maski river, a tributary of the Tungabhadra. A long sequence from the Palaeolithic through the South Indian Neolithic and Chalcolithic to the Megalithic Iron Age and early historic periods. The inscription that identified Ashoka, the single most consequential epigraphic discovery for Mauryan history.

notes.name: Masrur Rock-cut Temple
notes.note: Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, on a sandstone ridge above the Beas valley. Monolithic rock-cut complex of about the 8th century CE. The only monolithic rock-cut temple complex in north India, the Nagara counterpart of the Deccan's Dravida excavations.

notes.name: Mathura
notes.note: On the right bank of the Yamuna in western Uttar Pradesh. Dated c. 800-400 BCE. One of the largest PGW sites, and the clearest case of a PGW village growing without a break into a metropolis.

notes.name: Meerut
notes.note: Western Uttar Pradesh, in the Ganga-Yamuna doab on the Hindon. C. 2000-1500 BCE. The core OCP district, and the tract that yields both the anthropomorph hoards and the late Harappan graves that date them.

notes.name: Mehrangarh
notes.note: Jodhpur, Rajasthan. Notably Jaswant Singh and Ajit Singh in the 17th and 18th centuries. The Rathore stronghold of Marwar, and the centre of the longest Rajput resistance to Aurangzeb. When Jaswant Singh died in 1678.

notes.name: Mehrauli
notes.note: The Iron Pillar. A Sanskrit inscription in Gupta Brahmi of the 4th-5th century CE naming a king Chandra. The most famous metallurgical object of ancient India, and a political record of Gupta expansion into Bengal and the north-west.

notes.name: Mehrgarh
notes.note: On the Kachi plain of Balochistan, Pakistan. Occupied from about 7000 BCE to 2600 BCE. The earliest farming settlement in South Asia, and the site that settled the question of where Indian agriculture came from.

notes.name: Mehtakhedi
notes.note: Khargone district, Madhya Pradesh, in the middle Narmada valley. Upper Palaeolithic. Mehtakheri has produced one of the earliest dated microblade industries in India, and is therefore central to the debate on when microlithic technology.

notes.name: Melur - Mannikavasagar
notes.note: Associated with Tiruvathavur near Melur, Madurai district, Tamil Nadu. Manikkavachakar is generally placed in the 9th century CE. The finest devotional poet in Tamil, and one of the four Samayacharyas who shaped Shaiva Siddhanta.

notes.name: Mirpur
notes.note: Sirohi district, southern Rajasthan, near Abu Road in the Aravalli foothills. Built in white marble and usually assigned to the 9th-10th centuries CE under Rajput patronage. Claimed as the oldest marble monument in Rajasthan, and the precursor to Dilwara.

notes.name: Modhera
notes.note: Mehsana district, Gujarat, on the left bank of the Pushpavati. I.e. 1026-27 CE. The best-preserved sun temple in western India, and a building designed around the movement of the sun itself.

notes.name: Mogara Hills
