notes.note: Western Rajasthan, on the eastern fringe of the Thar desert. Middle and Upper Palaeolithic, and Mesolithic. The hill appears to have been a factory site where tools of all four phases were made.

notes.name: Mohenjodaro
notes.note: Larkana district, Sindh. Found by R. D. Banerji (1922), excavated by John Marshall. The fullest expression of Harappan urbanism, the benchmark against which every other site is described. Two mounds: a smaller but higher western mound, the citadel.

notes.name: Mukhalingam
notes.note: Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh, on the Vamsadhara river close to the Odisha border. Capital of the Eastern Gangas from about the 8th century until Anantavarman Chodaganga shifted the seat to Cuttack in the 12th. The capital of the dynasty that built Puri and Konark.

notes.name: Multan
notes.note: Southern Punjab, Pakistan. Described by Xuanzang in the 7th century and by Al-Biruni before Mahmud of Ghazni destroyed it. The seat of the Suhrawardi order in India, the counter-model to Chishti practice, and the Sultanate's principal western trade city.

notes.name: Mundigak
notes.note: About 55 km north-west of Kandahar in southern Afghanistan, on the Kushk-i-Nakhud river. Running from about 4000 BCE to the early 2nd millennium. A major regional centre outside the Indus system, and evidence that monumental building was not a Harappan monopoly.

notes.name: Muziris
notes.note: Sangam-age Muchiri, on the Periyar near Kodungallur (Cranganore), Ernakulam district, Kerala. Active from about the 1st century BCE to the 4th century CE and referred to into the medieval period. The western terminus of the Roman pepper trade.

notes.name: Mylapore
notes.note: Now a quarter of Chennai. Active under the Pallavas and Cholas and trading into the medieval centuries. The focus of the St Thomas tradition in India, and the Portuguese settlement that Madras grew up beside.

notes.name: Nabadwip - Chaitanya
notes.note: Nadia district, West Bengal. A seat of Sanskrit learning from the 11th century. Two distinct claims on the same town, the most rigorous school of Sanskrit logic in late medieval India.

notes.name: Nachna Kuthra
notes.note: Panna district, Madhya Pradesh, on the Vindhyan plateau north of the Ken. Gupta period, c. late 5th century CE. The Gupta temple at the moment it acquires height and an ambulatory, the step between Tigawa and Deogarh.

notes.name: Nagaon - Shankardev
notes.note: Bordowa in Nagaon district, Assam. Taught through the late Ahom and Koch period. The founder of Assamese neo-Vaishnavism, and the most complete case of a religious movement creating a regional culture whole.

notes.name: Nagar
notes.note: Also called Karkota Nagar, Tonk district, Rajasthan. An early historic settlement of roughly the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE. The type-site for the tribal republics, the ganas and sanghas that were not monarchies, known mainly through their coins.

notes.name: Nagarjuna Hills or Vijaypuri
notes.note: Ancient Vijayapuri. C. 225-325 CE. The most completely excavated early historic city in India, and the most completely lost. More than thirty Buddhist establishments were recorded, with mahachaityas.

notes.name: Nagarjunakonda
notes.note: Palnadu (formerly Guntur) district, Andhra Pradesh. A sequence running from the palaeolithic. The one site where the megalithic phase can be read directly against both a neolithic village below it and an early historic city above.

notes.name: Nageshwar
notes.note: Near Dwarka in Devbhumi Dwarka (formerly Jamnagar) district, Gujarat. A single-period mature Harappan settlement, c. 2500-2000 BCE. The purest example of a Harappan single-craft settlement, founded to work one raw material and abandoned with it.

notes.name: Naikund
notes.note: About 40 km north-east of Nagpur in Vidarbha, Maharashtra. Vidarbha megalithic, with calibrated ranges of 800-420 BCE and 785-410 BCE. Supplies the dates for the Vidarbha megaliths and the clearest iron-smelting workshop of the Indian iron age.

notes.name: Nal
notes.note: Sohr Damb, near the village of Nal in Khuzdar district, Balochistan, Pakistan. A Chalcolithic settlement of roughly the 4th and 3rd millennia BCE. The source of the finest painted pottery in South Asian prehistory.

notes.name: Nalanda
notes.note: Bargaon, Nalanda district, Bihar. Founded by Kumaragupta I in the 5th century CE (c. 415-455). The first residential university in the world, and the institution that separates monastic learning from the individual-teacher tradition of Taxila.

notes.name: Nanaghat
notes.note: The Naneghat pass through the Sahyadris, Junnar taluk, Pune district, Maharashtra. A Brahmi inscription in Prakrit of about the 1st century BCE. The founding document of Satavahana history, and the earliest attestation of the numerals from which modern digits descend.

notes.name: Nankana Sahib - Nanak Dev
notes.note: Formerly Talwandi, in Sheikhupura district, Punjab, Pakistan. The birthplace of Guru Nanak, 1469-1539. The origin of Sikhism, and of a religious teaching that was institutional as well as devotional from the start.

notes.name: Naraina - Dadu
notes.note: Jaipur district, Rajasthan. Dadu Dayal, 1544-1603, a cotton-carder by trade, probably of Muslim birth. The founder of the Dadupanth, and one of the clearest cases of a nirguna teacher building a lasting order.

notes.name: Narhan
notes.note: Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh, on the northern bank of the Sarayu (Ghaghara). A cultural sequence stretching from the second half of the 2nd millennium BCE to the 7th century CE. The type site of the Narhan culture, whose sequence is repeated at many places across the middle Ganga plains.

notes.name: Nartiang
notes.note: West Jaintia Hills district, Meghalaya. A living megalithic tradition rather than a prehistoric one: the stones of the monolith park were raised by Jaintia chieftains from about the 16th century CE onwards. The largest single collection of standing monoliths in India.

notes.name: Nashik
notes.note: On the Godavari in northern Maharashtra. Lower Palaeolithic tools recovered in a stratigraphic context. Nashik contributes one of the stratified river-section profiles on which H. D. Sankalia and his successors built the Palaeolithic sequence of the Deccan.

notes.name: Nashik Pandavleni Caves
notes.note: The Trirashmi hills, about 8 km south of Nashik, Maharashtra, above the Godavari. Twenty-four caves cut between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE. The single most important epigraphic site of the Deccan, the caves are read for their inscriptions more than for their architecture.

notes.name: Navdatoli
notes.note: On the southern bank of the Narmada opposite Maheshwar. A Chalcolithic settlement of the Malwa culture, about 1700-1200 BCE. Navdatoli has produced a greater variety of cereals than any other excavated site in India, which makes it the standard reference for Chalcolithic agriculture.

notes.name: Newasa
notes.note: Nevasa, Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra, on the Pravara river, a tributary of the Godavari. One mound with two widely separated occupations. The type site of the Indian Middle Palaeolithic, and one of the principal sources for Chalcolithic burial and belief in the Deccan.

notes.name: Nirppeyarru
notes.note: A Pallava port town of the Tamil coast known from inscriptions rather than from surviving remains. Pallava period, c. 7th-9th centuries CE. Evidence that the Pallavas worked a coastline of several harbours rather than a single port.

notes.name: Nittur and Udegolam
notes.note: Two rock sites a few kilometres apart in Bellary district, Karnataka. C. 258-257 BCE. Two of the five inscriptions that name Ashoka outright, and a reminder that the corpus is still growing.

notes.name: Odai
notes.note: Villupuram district, Tamil Nadu, near Tiruvakkarai in the South Pennar tract. Middle to Upper Palaeolithic with microliths. One of the very few hominid fossil localities in the subcontinent, marked alongside Hathnora on standard maps of hominid discoveries in South Asia.

notes.name: Ojiyana
notes.note: Bhilwara district, Rajasthan, on the Khari river in the Banas system. An Ahar or Banas culture Chalcolithic settlement. One of the more recently excavated Banas culture sites, and unusual in being built on a hill slope.

notes.name: Padari
notes.note: Padri (Kerala-no-dhoro), near Talaja in Bhavnagar district, Gujarat. Period I is an early Harappan 'Padri ware' phase, c. 3000-2600 BCE. Established that Gujarat had a well-developed early Harappan horizon of its own, indigenous and distinct from the Amri-Nal tradition of Sindh.

notes.name: Padmavati
notes.note: Pawaya, ancient Padmavati, Gwalior district, Madhya Pradesh. Capital of the Nagas of Padmavati in the 3rd-4th centuries CE. The seat of one of the regional powers that filled the gap between two empires, and the dynasty Samudragupta had to remove.

notes.name: Pahalgam
notes.note: In the Liddar valley of Anantnag district, Kashmir. Lower Palaeolithic. The handaxe recovered here is one of a very small number of Palaeolithic finds from Kashmir, where cold conditions. The Kashmir Upper Palaeolithic has been dated to about 18,000 BP and coincides with the onset of a milder climate.

notes.name: Paisra
notes.note: In the Kharagpur forests near Munger, Bihar. A Lower Palaeolithic living and working floor. One of the rare Lower Palaeolithic sites in India to yield structural evidence of dwellings. Eight post-holes were found.

notes.name: Paithan - Eknath
notes.note: On the north bank of the Godavari, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra. Worked at Paithan during the Nizam Shahi and early Mughal period in the Deccan. The saint who recovered the Varkari textual tradition and pushed it furthest on caste.

notes.name: Paithan or Pratishthana
notes.note: Ancient Pratishthana, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra, on the north bank of the Godavari. Capital of the Satavahanas from about the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE. The southern terminus of the Dakshinapatha, and the capital of the dynasty that made the Deccan a political unit.

notes.name: Paiyampalli
notes.note: Tirupattur district, northern Tamil Nadu. A South Indian Neolithic settlement with a Megalithic phase above it. The southern limit of the Neolithic cattle-keeping culture, and a key site for the domestication of Indian pulses.

notes.name: Palakkad
notes.note: Kerala, at the Palghat gap. Palaeolithic surface finds. Choppers and scrapers made of quartz have been found in the district, among the few Palaeolithic finds reported from Kerala. The Palghat gap itself explains the importance of the district.

notes.name: Palavoy
notes.note: In the Anantapur region of Andhra Pradesh. A South Indian Neolithic site with four ashmounds. An ashmound cluster, and the evidence that these were regional gathering places rather than single-village features.

notes.name: Palkigundu and gavimath
notes.note: Two rock sites near Koppal in Koppal district, Karnataka. C. 258-257 BCE. Part of the dense southern cluster of Minor Rock Edicts. Minor Rock Edict I preaches dhamma and the duty of exerting oneself in it.

notes.name: Pallavaram
notes.note: Near Chennai, formerly Madras, Tamil Nadu. Lower Palaeolithic (Acheulian). In the summer of 1863 Robert Bruce Foote, an officer of the Geological Survey of India on routine survey duty. Foote went on to find and study many more stone tools and made major contributions to research on Indian prehistory.

notes.name: Pandharpur Vitthala temple
notes.note: Solapur district, Maharashtra, on the right bank of the Bhima. The core shrine belongs to the Yadava period. The centre of the Varkari sampradaya, the most important bhakti site in Maharashtra.

notes.name: Pandu Rajar dhibi
notes.note: Barddhaman district, West Bengal. A Chalcolithic settlement excavated by P. C. Dasgupta from 1962. The type-site of the Bengal Chalcolithic, and the first excavation to establish that Bengal had a pre-iron settled culture at all.

notes.name: Panguraria Minor RE
notes.note: At the foot of the Saru Maru hills in Sehore district, Madhya Pradesh. Two inscriptions in Brahmi and Prakrit. The only Ashokan inscription that looks back to the emperor's life before he was emperor.

notes.name: Parasnath
notes.note: Also called Shikharji or Sammed Shikhar, Giridih district, Jharkhand. Generally placed in the 8th century BCE. The holiest Jaina pilgrimage site of all, where twenty of the twenty-four tirthankaras are held to have attained moksha.

notes.name: Paro Monastery
notes.note: Paro Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest, in the Paro valley of western Bhutan. The Taktsang Senge Samdup cave is held to be where Padmasambhava meditated in the 8th century CE. The defining monument of Bhutanese Buddhism, and the eastern end of the Padmasambhava tradition that began in Indian Vajrayana.

notes.name: Patliputra
notes.note: Pataliputra, modern Patna, Bihar, on the strip between the Ganga and the Son. Founded as a fort by the Magadhan king Udayin c. 460 BCE and made the capital in place of Rajagriha. The capital of the first Indian empire.

notes.name: Patne
notes.note: Jalgaon district, Maharashtra, in the Tapi valley. A stratigraphic sequence of Middle Palaeolithic, Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic tools. Patne is the single most important Indian site for Upper Palaeolithic art and personal ornament.

notes.name: Pattadakal
notes.note: Bagalkot district, Karnataka. The Early Chalukya coronation site. The one site where the Nagara and Dravida orders stand side by side, built by the same dynasty at the same time.

notes.name: Pavapuri
notes.note: Pawapuri, Nalanda district, Bihar. Traditionally in 527 BCE by Jaina reckoning. The site of Mahavira's death, and the eastern anchor of the Jaina sacred geography of Magadha. Jaina tradition holds that so much earth was taken from around the cremation site by devotees that a tank formed.

notes.name: Penukonda
notes.note: Sri Sathya Sai district, Andhra Pradesh. A Vijayanagara stronghold from the 14th century. The proof that Vijayanagara did not end in 1565, the standard correction to the textbook date. The Aravidu dynasty ruled from Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore for nearly a century after Talikota.

notes.name: Peshawar
notes.note: The Peshawar valley, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Middle and Upper Palaeolithic. Sanghao provides the best stratified cave sequence for the Middle and Upper Palaeolithic in the north-west of the subcontinent. The deposit is over 3 m thick and yielded thousands of stone tools, including chipped stone.

notes.name: Piklihal
notes.note: Raichur district, Karnataka, on granite hills near the Krishna in the Raichur doab. A South Indian Neolithic settlement dated from about 2700 BCE. One of the two sites on which the interpretation of the southern Neolithic as a cattle-keeping culture was built.

notes.name: Pirak Late Harappa
notes.note: In the Kachi plain of Baluchistan near Sibi. Period I begins c. 1800 BCE and Periods II-III run to about 600 BCE. The site that documents the beginning of double cropping and the earliest secure horse in South Asia.

notes.name: Pitalkhora Caves
notes.note: In a ravine of the Satmala range of the Western Ghats near Kannad. Of c. 2nd century BCE. The earliest monumental sculpture in the western Deccan caves, older than Karle and contemporary with Bhaja.

notes.name: Porivarai
notes.note: In the Karikkiyur complex of the Nilgiri hills near Kotagiri, Tamil Nadu. Rock paintings assigned broadly to the late Neolithic and megalithic periods. The principal rock art site of the Nilgiris, the southern extremity of the Indian painted-shelter tradition.

notes.name: Porkalam
notes.note: Near Kunnamkulam in Thrissur district, Kerala. Broadly c. 1000-100 BCE. The type site for the distinctive laterite megalithic forms of Kerala, found nowhere else in India. A kudakkal or umbrella stone: four clinostatic laterite slabs capped by a dressed hemispherical stone.

notes.name: Potali or Bodana
notes.note: Usually identified with Bodhan on the Godavari in Nizamabad district, Telangana. A mahajanapada capital of the 6th-4th centuries BCE. Marks the southern limit of the mahajanapada map and the Deccan end of the Dakshinapatha.

notes.name: Prabhas Patan
notes.note: Better known as Somnath. The Chalcolithic phase is dated about 2000-1400 BCE and gives its name to Prabhas ware. A post-Harappan Chalcolithic culture of coastal Saurashtra that shows how Harappan traditions were absorbed into regional cultures after the decline of the cities.

notes.name: Pragjyotishpura
notes.note: Identified with Guwahati, Assam, on the Brahmaputra where the river narrows between hills. C. 350-650 CE. The seat of the earliest historical kingdom of the north-east, and the point at which Assam enters the mainstream Indian record.

notes.name: Prahladpur
notes.note: Varanasi district, Uttar Pradesh. Period I is a pre-NBPW black-slipped ware phase, Period II is NBPW. A small dig of large consequence, one of the excavations that fixed the ceramic sequence of the middle Ganga.

notes.name: Puhar
notes.note: Mayiladuthurai district, Tamil Nadu, where the Kaveri enters the Bay of Bengal. C. 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE. The best-described city of early Tamilakam, a place where literature gives a town plan that archaeology can then test.

notes.name: Pulwama
notes.note: Awantipora, Pulwama district, Jammu and Kashmir. R. 855-883 CE. The Utpala capital, and the setting of the most celebrated feat of engineering in Kashmir's history. Kalhana's Rajatarangini records that Avantivarman's engineer Suyya regulated the Jhelum where it was choked at Baramulla.

notes.name: Puri
notes.note: Odisha, on the Bay of Bengal coast south of the Mahanadi delta. The Govardhana matha is assigned to Adi Shankara in the 8th century. One of the Char Dham, Shankara's eastern seat, and the place where the Jagannath cult became the ideology of a state.

notes.name: Purushapura
notes.note: Peshawar, ancient Purushapura. R. from c. 127 CE. The capital from which the Kushanas ruled an empire spanning Central Asia and northern India, and the centre of Gandhara Buddhism. The great stupa Kanishka raised at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri was described by Faxian and Xuanzang as the tallest structure they had seen anywhere.

notes.name: Pushkalvati
notes.note: The mounds of Bala Hisar and Shaikhan Dheri at Charsadda, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Bala Hisar excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1958. The north-western terminus of the NBPW map, and a city planned on a grid two centuries before Sirkap.

notes.name: Pushkar
notes.note: Ajmer district, Rajasthan, around a lake in a hollow of the Aravallis. An ancient tirtha named in the Mahabharata. The principal Brahma temple in India, the one place where a god of the classical triad has almost no independent cult.

notes.name: Pushpagiri
notes.note: The Langudi and Assia hills of Jajpur district, Odisha. A Buddhist monastic complex active from about the 1st-3rd centuries CE to the 11th-12th. The principal Buddhist university of eastern India outside Bihar, and the centre where Vajrayana takes shape.

notes.name: Quetta
notes.note: Balochistan, Pakistan. The Quetta valley carries one of the longest cultural sequences in South Asia. The corridor through which farming, and later people and goods, entered the subcontinent. Mehrgarh, excavated by Jean-Francois Jarrige, is the earliest farming settlement known in South Asia: mud-brick houses.

notes.name: Rabatak
notes.note: Near Surkh Kotal in Baghlan province, northern Afghanistan, ancient Bactria. C. 127 CE, the opening of the Kushana empire's greatest phase. The find that settled the Kushana genealogy after a century of scholarly argument, the most consequential Indian epigraphic discovery of recent decades.

notes.name: Raigad
notes.note: Raigad district, Maharashtra. Taken by Shivaji from the Chandrarao More of Javli in 1656. The seat of the Maratha state, and the setting of the coronation that turned a rebellion into a kingdom.

notes.name: Rajgir
notes.note: Nalanda district, Bihar, in a valley ringed by five hills on the Banganga. The old city of Girivraja with its cyclopean stone wall is pre-Mauryan. The capital from which Magadha's ascendancy was built, and the only major mahajanapada capital defended by stone.

notes.name: Rajim
notes.note: Gariaband district, Chhattisgarh, at the confluence of the Mahanadi. Founded by Vilasatunga of the Nala dynasty in about the 7th-8th century CE. The main surviving monument of the Nala dynasty, and a Vaishnava centre in the Mahanadi valley between the Deccan and Odisha.

notes.name: Rajouri or Rajapura
notes.note: Rajapura. A mahajanapada of the 6th-4th centuries BCE. The north-western corner of the mahajanapada map, and a corporation of the frontier rather than a kingdom of the plains. The Mahabharata records Karna's defeat of the Kambojas at Rajapura.

notes.name: Rajula Mandagiri
notes.note: Near Pattikonda in Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh. C. 258-257 BCE. One of the southern pair of sites, with Yerragudi, 40 km away, that carries both Minor Rock Edicts together. Minor Rock Edict II is the more important of the two for the content of dhamma.

notes.name: Rakhigarhi
notes.note: Hisar district, Haryana, on the dry Ghaggar-Drishadvati plain. Early Harappan Period I, mature Harappan c. 2600-1900 BCE. The largest Harappan city in India, with all three phases represented, and the source of the first ancient genome from the civilisation.

notes.name: Ramadevra
notes.note: Ramdevra, also called Runicha, Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan. A Tanwar Rajput chieftain of the early 15th century. A regional saint venerated across religious and caste lines, the best western Indian example of folk devotion that no orthodoxy controls.

notes.name: Rampurwa
notes.note: West Champaran district, Bihar. C. 243-242 BCE. The finest surviving Mauryan animal capital, and the clearest evidence of Achaemenid and Hellenistic motifs in Mauryan art. The Rampurva bull, carved in the round in sandstone with the characteristic Mauryan polish.

notes.name: Rana Gundai
notes.note: Rana Ghundai, Loralai district, north-eastern Balochistan, Pakistan. Spanning roughly the 4th to the 2nd millennia BCE. The excavation that gave Balochistan its first chronology, and the origin of a long-running argument about destruction levels.

notes.name: Rangpur
notes.note: On the Bhadar river in the Saurashtra peninsula of Gujarat. A Harappan and post-Harappan sequence. Rangpur supplied the stratigraphic sequence on which the idea of a Late Harappan phase in Gujarat was built.

notes.name: Ranthambore
notes.note: Sawai Madhopur district, Rajasthan. Probably in the 10th century. The site of Alauddin Khalji's first great Rajput siege, and of the jauhar tradition's earliest well-documented instance. Hammira Deva's refusal to surrender Mongol rebels who had taken refuge with him gave Alauddin his pretext.

notes.name: Ratanpura
notes.note: North Gujarat. A Mesolithic and Chalcolithic dune settlement of the Anarta tradition. One of the cluster of north Gujarat dune sites that define the Anarta tradition. Loteshwar is the excavated type-site, Ratanpura one of its neighbours.

notes.name: Rehman Dheri
notes.note: Dera Ismail Khan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. An Early Harappan town of about 3300-2100 BCE. One of the earliest planned settlements in South Asia, laid out on a grid several centuries before the Mature Harappan cities.

notes.name: Renigunta, Chitoor
notes.note: Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, on the Swarnamukhi drainage below the Seshachalam hills. An Upper Palaeolithic industry with a Mesolithic phase above it. A reference site for the Upper Palaeolithic blade-and-burin industry in south India, and for the transition into the Mesolithic.

notes.name: Rojdi
notes.note: Rajkot district, Gujarat. G. L. Possehl and M. H. Raval (1982-86). Type site of the Sorath Harappan of Saurashtra, and the clearest proof that the Harappan 'decline' was regional rather than universal.

notes.name: Ropar
notes.note: Punjab. The first excavation undertaken in independent India. Supplies the standard stratified sequence from the Harappan to the medieval period in the Sutlej valley. Harappan levels with typical red ware, chert blades, steatite seals, beads, terracotta cakes and bangles.

notes.name: Runkata - Surdas
notes.note: Near Agra on the Yamuna in Uttar Pradesh. Surdas, c. 1478-1583 by tradition, was blind from birth or early childhood. The greatest poet of Braj Bhasha, and the figure through whom Krishna devotion became a literature of childhood and maternal love.

notes.name: Rupnagar
notes.note: On the left bank of the Sutlej in Punjab. Period II is PGW. Fixes the PGW-after-a-break pattern that stands against the Bhagwanpura overlap, the two together frame the Harappan-Vedic argument.

notes.name: Rupnath
notes.note: Katni district, Madhya Pradesh. C. 258-257 BCE. One of the three texts James Prinsep worked on when he deciphered Brahmi. Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi in 1837, using Rupnath, Sahasram, Bairat and the Delhi and Girnar texts.

notes.name: Sabarmati Valley
notes.note: The Sabarmati valley of north Gujarat, together with its Orsang and Karjan tributaries. Lower Palaeolithic. Lower Palaeolithic tools have been found throughout these valleys. Lower Palaeolithic and later artefacts have also been found all along the Konkan coast as far as Goa.

notes.name: Saipal
notes.note: Saipai, Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, in the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab. Chalcolithic, broadly of the 2nd millennium BCE. Saipai is one of the few sites where Copper Hoard objects have been recovered in a stratified excavation alongside Ochre-Coloured Pottery.

notes.name: Sambhar
notes.note: Jaipur district, Rajasthan, on the shore of Sambhar Salt Lake. Capital of the Chahamanas (Chauhans) from about the 7th century until the seat moved to Ajmer under Ajayaraja in the 12th. The Chauhan homeland, and a salt resource that explains why the site was worth holding.

notes.name: Sanchi
notes.note: Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh. Stupa 1 was commissioned by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE as a brick mound. The best-preserved and most complete early Buddhist stupa in India. The Ashokan pillar beside the southern gateway is of finely polished sandstone with a four-lion capital.

notes.name: Sanganakallu
notes.note: Ballari district, Karnataka, on granite hills near the Tungabhadra in the Raichur doab. A long sequence from a Mesolithic microlithic phase through the South Indian Neolithic. The type-site of the South Indian Neolithic, and the location of stone axe production on an industrial scale.

notes.name: Sanghol
notes.note: Fatehgarh Sahib district, Punjab. A multi-period mound with late Harappan, its great phase is Kushana. The largest single hoard of Mathura sculpture ever found, and the proof that Mathura workshops exported finished stone hundreds of kilometres north.

notes.name: Sankissa
notes.note: Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh, on the Kali Nadi, the ancient Ikshumati. Occupied from about the 6th century BCE. One of the eight great places of Buddhist pilgrimage, and the only Ashokan pillar to carry an elephant capital.

notes.name: Sannati
notes.note: Chitapur taluk, Kalaburagi (Gulbarga) district, Karnataka, on the left bank of the Bhima. C. 257-256 BCE. The only place outside Kalinga where the two Separate Edicts have been found. Sannati shows the same text in the Deccan.

notes.name: Sanur
notes.note: Near Tindivanam in the old Chingleput district of northern Tamil Nadu. Placed by its excavators in the last centuries BCE and the early centuries CE. The standard published Tamil Nadu megalithic excavation, and the site that defined the dolmenoid cist with a sarcophagus, the illustration reproduced in most textbooks.

notes.name: Sarai Khola
notes.note: In the Taxila valley of Punjab, Pakistan. Four periods excavated by the Pakistan Department of Archaeology. The only site that carries the Taxila region from its Neolithic beginnings through to the historical city, a four-thousand-year sequence in one mound.

notes.name: Sarai Nahar Rai
notes.note: Pratapgarh district, Uttar Pradesh. A radiocarbon determination of c. 8400 BCE is often quoted. The first excavated Mesolithic cemetery in the Ganga plain, and the site that produced direct evidence of violence between hunter-gatherers.

notes.name: Sarnath
notes.note: Ancient Isipatana, the Migadaya or Deer Park, 10 km north-east of Varanasi. C. 528 BCE. Where the Sangha came into being, and where the two most reproduced objects in modern India were made.

notes.name: Sarutaru
notes.note: Kamrup district, Assam. A Neolithic occupation broadly of the 2nd millennium BCE. The Neolithic of the Brahmaputra plain, showing that the north-eastern tool tradition extended out of the hills onto the valley floor.

notes.name: Sasaram
notes.note: Rohtas district, Bihar. The tomb of Sher Shah Suri, r. 1540-1545. The finest tomb of the Indo-Afghan tradition, and the burial place of the administrator the Mughals copied. The tomb is the culmination of the Lodi-Sur octagonal type: an octagon within a square terrace.

notes.name: Saspul Caves
notes.note: Saspol (Saspochhe) caves, Leh district, Ladakh. Five man-made caves painted in the 13th-15th centuries CE. A fusion of the Indian-Kashmiri manner of Alchi with the Tibetan style that replaced it, the transition caught mid-way.

notes.name: Savalda
notes.note: In the Tapi valley of northern Maharashtra. Going back to the 3rd millennium BCE. Savalda ware is the diagnostic pottery of the first agricultural communities of Maharashtra, and is remarkable for painted designs that depict tools and weapons.

notes.name: Sebalgiri
notes.note: Selbalgre, West Garo Hills district, Meghalaya. A Mesolithic and Neolithic occupation in the Garo hills. One of very few excavated prehistoric sites in the north-east, and evidence for animal keeping in the hills.

notes.name: Senaur
notes.note: Senuar. Four periods of occupation: Period I is Neolithic and Neolithic-Chalcolithic. The most important of the excavated Neolithic-Chalcolithic sites of the Bihar plains. Carbonised grains show that two crops a year were grown.

notes.name: Senuwar
notes.note: Rohtas district, Bihar. Period IA is Neolithic, from about 2200 BCE, Period II is Chalcolithic. The best-dated and most thoroughly sampled Neolithic sequence in the middle Ganga plain, the reference against which the disputed Belan valley dates are judged.

notes.name: Shah-e-Hamadan (Srinagar)
notes.note: The Khanqah-e-Moula or Shah-e-Hamadan mosque. Built in 1395 by Sultan Sikandar in memory of Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani. The masterpiece of Kashmiri wooden architecture, and the monument of the Sufi credited with reshaping the valley's economy as well as its religion.

notes.name: Shahbazgarhi
notes.note: Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. C. 257-256 BCE. The north-western limit of the Major Rock Edicts, and the fullest evidence that the empire published in the local script. The text is divided between two rocks on the hillside.

notes.name: Banskhera (Shahjahanpur)
notes.note: Shahjahanpur district, Uttar Pradesh. C. 628 CE, 606-647 CE. One of only two known charters of Harsha, and the rarest kind of document in Indian history, a royal autograph. The plate records the grant of a village to two brahmanas, Bhatta Vatasvamin and Bhatta Shivadevasvamin.

notes.name: Shalozan
notes.note: In the upper Kurram valley on the Pakistan-Afghanistan frontier (Kurram district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa). A copper hoard findspot of the 2nd millennium BCE. Marks the westernmost extent of the copper hoard distribution, and the point at which the Indian series meets the Iranian and Central Asian one.

notes.name: Shamalji
notes.note: Shamlaji, Aravalli district, Gujarat. Two distinct phases. The type-site of a recognised regional sculptural school, and a Vaishnava tirtha on a long-used trade route. The "Shamlaji school" of the 6th century, Vishnu, Matrika and Skanda images in grey schist.

notes.name: Sharda Peeth
notes.note: In the Neelum (Kishanganga) valley about 140 km from Srinagar. A seat of learning and a Shakti shrine attested from about the 6th century CE and flourishing under the Karkota. The centre that made Kashmir the byword for Sanskrit scholarship, Sharada Desha, the land of the goddess of learning.

notes.name: Shatrunjaya
notes.note: Bhavnagar district, Gujarat. A tirtha from early centuries in tradition. The largest temple city in the world, some 863 shrines on one hill, and the supreme tirtha of the Svetambara Jains.

notes.name: Shivalik
notes.note: The Siwalik or Shivalik range, the outermost range of the Himalayas. Lower Palaeolithic. The Siwaliks supply the greatest claimed time-depth for stone tools anywhere in the subcontinent, though these very early dates remain debated.

notes.name: Shortugai
notes.note: In Darqad of Takhar province, north-eastern Afghanistan. Mature Harappan, c. 2200-2000 BCE, an isolated Harappan colony. The only true Harappan trading outpost outside the subcontinent, and the strongest single evidence for organised long-distance procurement.

notes.name: Shravanabelagol
notes.note: Hassan district, Karnataka. A Jaina centre from about the 3rd century BCE in tradition and certainly from the Western Ganga period. The principal Digambara Jaina site in India, and home to the tallest free-standing monolithic statue in the world.

notes.name: Shravasti
notes.note: On the south bank of the Rapti, the ancient Achiravati. Identified by Sir Alexander Cunningham in 1863. A Mahajanapada capital whose PGW village underlies one of the greatest Buddhist centres in India.

notes.name: Shri Mahavirji
notes.note: Karauli district, eastern Rajasthan. A modern Digambara pilgrimage complex grown around an image of Mahavira said to have been recovered from a mound at the village of Chandangaon in the 18th century. The principal Digambara pilgrimage centre of Rajasthan.

notes.name: Sialkot
notes.note: Ancient Sagala or Sakala, in Punjab, Pakistan. R. c. 155-130 BCE. The capital of the most successful Indo-Greek king, and the setting of the one text in which a Greek ruler debates Indian philosophy.

notes.name: Sibsagar
notes.note: Sivasagar, upper Assam. 18th century. The architecture of the one Indian state that held off the Mughals for a century, and a distinct Ahom building idiom. The Shivadol rises about 33 m and is among the tallest Shiva temples in India.

notes.name: Sigiriya Caves
notes.note: Matale district, central Sri Lanka. Caves around the rock carry drip-ledges and Brahmi inscriptions of c. 3rd century BCE-1st century CE. The best-preserved example of early Asian urban planning, and the closest surviving relative of the Ajanta painting tradition.

notes.name: Singhbhum
notes.note: On the Chhotanagpur plateau of Jharkhand, in the Subarnarekha basin. Lower Palaeolithic. The river valleys and foothills of the Chhotanagpur plateau and the adjoining areas of West Bengal have yielded Lower Palaeolithic tools.

notes.name: Sirpur
notes.note: Mahasamund district, Chhattisgarh, on the left bank of the Mahanadi. 6th-8th centuries CE, at its height under Mahashivagupta Balarjuna (c. 595-655 CE). A capital where Buddhist, Jaina and Brahmanical establishments stood together, and the finest surviving brick temple of the Deccan fringe.

notes.name: Sisupalgarh
notes.note: On the southern edge of Bhubaneswar, Khordha district, Odisha. Period I, c. 400-200 BCE, Period II, c. 200 BCE-100 CE. The best-preserved planned fortified city of early historic India, the one whose full plan can still be walked.

notes.name: Sisupalgarh or Dhauli
notes.note: The Dhauli rock. C. 257-256 BCE. The earliest rock-cut sculpture in India stands above the edicts that are Ashoka's answer to the war he fought here. Major Rock Edicts 11, 12 and 13 are omitted, as at Jaugada.

notes.name: Sitabinji
notes.note: Keonjhar district, Odisha, on the Sita river in the upper Baitarani basin. Carrying a tempera mural usually dated to the 6th-7th centuries CE. The only surviving early mural painting in eastern India, and one of very few anywhere outside Ajanta, Bagh and Sittanavasal.

notes.name: Sittanavasal
notes.note: Pudukkottai district, Tamil Nadu. Two phases. The best surviving Jaina paintings in India, and evidence for Jaina monasticism in the far south from the last centuries BCE. The paintings, in fresco-secco on lime plaster, show a lotus pond with elephants, buffaloes, fish.

notes.name: Sohan Valley
notes.note: The Soan or Sohan river in the Potwar plateau. The Soanian pebble tool tradition of the Lower Palaeolithic. The type region of the Soanian industry and the setting of the first systematic palaeo-environmental study in Indian prehistory.

notes.name: Sohgaura
notes.note: Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh. Generally assigned to the Mauryan period and argued by some to be pre-Ashokan. One of the two earliest Brahmi records in India, and the oldest documentary evidence of state famine relief anywhere in the subcontinent.

notes.name: Somapura
notes.note: Paharpur, Badalgachhi, Naogaon district, Bangladesh. C. 781-821 CE. The largest Buddhist monastery south of the Himalayas, and the source of a building form that spread across South-East Asia. A square of 281 m a side, with 177 monastic cells opening on to a courtyard.

notes.name: Somnath
notes.note: Prabhas Patan near Veraval, Gir Somnath district, Gujarat. The first of the twelve jyotirlingas. Less an architectural site than a historiographical one, the single best case study in how a medieval raid was turned into a modern narrative.

notes.name: Sonagiri
notes.note: Datia district, Madhya Pradesh. A Digambara Jaina temple hill with some seventy-seven temples on the summit and about twenty-six more in the village below. A siddha-kshetra of the Digambara tradition, and a clear example of the Indian temple-hill type.

notes.name: Sopara
notes.note: Nala Sopara, Palghar district, Maharashtra, on the Konkan coast north of Mumbai. C. 257-256 BCE. The only Major Rock Edict site on the western seaboard, the empire's window on the Arabian Sea trade.

notes.name: Sri Ranganathswami temple
notes.note: Tiruchirappalli district, Tamil Nadu. Attested from the Sangam period and built up continuously by the Cholas. The largest functioning Hindu temple complex in the world, and the doctrinal centre of Srivaishnavism.

notes.name: Sringeri
notes.note: Chikkamagaluru district, Karnataka. Traditionally the first of the four mathas founded by Adi Shankara in the 8th century. The southern seat of Advaita Vedanta, and the best-documented case of a monastic institution shaping the founding of a kingdom.

notes.name: Sriperumbudur - Ramanuja
notes.note: Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, in the flat country between Kanchipuram and the coast. Traditionally 1017-1137 CE. The origin of Vishishtadvaita, the philosophy that gave devotional religion an intellectual foundation, and of a practical challenge to caste exclusion.

notes.name: Srirangapatnam
notes.note: Mandya district, Karnataka, on an island formed where the Kaveri divides. Fortified in 1454 by Timmanna Nayaka under Vijayanagara. The capital of the state that fought the East India Company four times, the most formidable Indian opponent the Company faced in the south.

notes.name: Srivilliputur - Andal
notes.note: Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu. Generally placed in the 8th-9th centuries CE. The one female voice in the Alwar canon, and the author of a text still recited by millions every year.

notes.name: Sukta-koh
notes.note: Sotka Koh, near Pasni on the Makran coast of Baluchistan. A mature Harappan coastal station, c. 2500-1900 BCE. One of the two Harappan stations on the Makran coast, plotting the sea route westward to the Persian Gulf.

notes.name: Suktakagendor
notes.note: Sutkagendor, Gwadar district, Baluchistan. Mature Harappan, c. 2500-1900 BCE. Fixes the western limit of the civilisation and anchors its maritime route to the Persian Gulf. A citadel raised on a stone and mud-brick platform with a massive fortification wall and bastions.

notes.name: Suktimati
notes.note: Capital of the Chedi mahajanapada in the Bundelkhand-Baghelkhand tract between the Yamuna and the Narmada. A mahajanapada capital of the 6th-4th centuries BCE. The one mahajanapada capital that archaeology has never located, which is itself the examinable point about the limits of the list of sixteen.

notes.name: Sundargarh
notes.note: North-western Odisha. A district-wide prehistoric sequence rather than a single site: Palaeolithic and Mesolithic surface industries on the river terraces. One of the principal prehistoric regions of eastern India, and the source of a famously contested inscription.

notes.name: Surkotada
notes.note: Rapar taluka, eastern Kutch district, Gujarat. C. 2300-1700 BCE. A fortified regional centre or garrison town, and the source of the most-debated horse evidence in Indian archaeology.

notes.name: Suvarnagiri
notes.note: The "golden mountain", the southern provincial capital of the Maurya empire. A Mauryan provincial headquarters of the 3rd century BCE. The clearest evidence for the structure of Mauryan provincial government, a capital known entirely from being quoted in other people's edicts.

notes.name: Tabo Caves and monastery
notes.note: Spiti valley, Lahaul and Spiti district, Himachal Pradesh. Founded in 996 CE by Yeshe-O. Called the Ajanta of the Himalayas, and the best-preserved monument of the second diffusion of Buddhism from India into Tibet.

notes.name: Tagara or Ter
notes.note: Ter, ancient Tagara, Dharashiv (Osmanabad) district, Maharashtra. A trade town of the Satavahana period. One of the two inland markets the Periplus names for the whole Deccan, and the source of a famous piece of Indian export art.

notes.name: Takh-i Bhai Monastery
notes.note: Takht-i-Bahi, Mardan district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Founded in the 1st century CE. The most complete surviving Gandharan monastery, the one where the whole plan of a Buddhist establishment can still be read.

notes.name: Talaja - Narsinh Mehta
notes.note: Bhavnagar district, Gujarat. Lived under the Gujarat Sultanate. The founder of Gujarati literature, and the author of the hymn that became the anthem of the national movement. Vaishnava Jana To defines a Vaishnava entirely by conduct, one who feels another's pain.

notes.name: Talakadu
notes.note: Mysuru district, Karnataka. Capital of the Western Gangas from about the 6th century CE. The Western Ganga capital, and the pivot of the long contest between Chola and Hoysala for southern Karnataka.

notes.name: Tamluk or Tamralipti
notes.note: Purba Medinipur district, West Bengal. A Chalcolithic black-and-red ware level at the base. The exit point of the Mauryan trade route to the south and south-east, and one of the two great terracotta centres of early Bengal.

notes.name: Thatta
notes.note: Sindh, Pakistan. Arghuns and Tarkhans from the 14th century. One of the largest funerary landscapes in the world, and the point where Persian and Timurid tilework meets Gujarati stone carving.

notes.name: Tawang gompa Monastert
notes.note: Arunachal Pradesh. Founded in 1680-81 by Merak Lama Lodre Gyatso at the instance of the fifth Dalai Lama. The largest monastery in India and the second largest in the world after the Potala, and the eastern anchor of the Gelugpa order's reach.

notes.name: Taxila
notes.note: Rawalpindi district, Punjab, Pakistan. C. 6th-2nd centuries BCE (Achaemenid and Mauryan, with local NBPW and silver punch-marked coins). The textbook contrast between an organic Indian town and a Hellenistic grid, standing 500 m apart.

notes.name: Tekkalakote
notes.note: Ballari district, Karnataka, among granite hills near the Tungabhadra in the Raichur doab. A South Indian Neolithic settlement of roughly 2000-1200 BCE with a Chalcolithic overlap. A Neolithic hill settlement that produced gold, the earliest worked gold in the peninsula.

notes.name: Thanale Caves
notes.note: Sudhagad taluka, Raigad district, Maharashtra, in a Sahyadri ravine above the Konkan. Twenty-three caves of c. 2nd-1st centuries BCE. One of the oldest and least disturbed of the early Konkan cave groups, the plain monastic architecture that the great sites grew out of.

notes.name: Thanesar or Sthanisvara
notes.note: Ancient Sthanvishvara, Kurukshetra district, Haryana. Capital of the Pushyabhuti dynasty from the 6th century CE: Prabhakaravardhana. The seat from which Harsha's empire began, and a tirtha whose sanctity long predates any dynasty.

notes.name: Thanjavur
notes.note: Tamil Nadu, in the Kaveri delta on the Vadavaru branch. The Brihadishvara (Rajarajeshvara) temple was built by Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 CE. The only substantial survival of Chola mural painting, hidden for nine centuries under a later layer, and the high point of Dravida temple building.

notes.name: Thapli
notes.note: In the Garhwal Himalaya of Uttarakhand. A Neolithic settlement with later occupation. Evidence that the Himalayan valleys were settled by farming communities, not merely crossed by them. The site has yielded ground and polished stone tools.

notes.name: Thenmala
notes.note: Kollam district, Kerala, on the Kallada river in the Western Ghats. A Mesolithic occupation with wood charcoal dated to about 5000 BCE. One of the few dated Mesolithic sites in Kerala, and evidence that the Western Ghats forests were occupied rather than merely crossed.

notes.name: Thikse Monastery
notes.note: Leh district, Ladakh. Founded in the 15th century. The clearest surviving example of Tibetan tiered monastic architecture in India, and the seat of the Gelugpa in Ladakh. Twelve storeys of white-washed buildings climb the hill in ascending rank.

notes.name: Thirunandikkara
notes.note: Kanyakumari district, Tamil Nadu. A rock-cut cave temple of about the 8th-9th centuries CE. The oldest surviving murals in the Kerala style, the starting point of a painting tradition that runs to Mattancherry and Padmanabhapuram.

notes.name: Tigawa
notes.note: Katni district, Madhya Pradesh. Gupta period, c. 400-425 CE. The first stage of the Indian temple in stone: the simplest possible form, before the shikhara. No ambulatory and no tower, Percy Brown's Class I Gupta temple.

notes.name: Tilwara
notes.note: Barmer district, western Rajasthan, on the bank of the Luni. A Mesolithic settlement with two cultural phases. The evidence base for animal domestication among Mesolithic communities of western India. The faunal remains include domesticated humped cattle, Bos indicus, alongside wild species, goat, canine, pig.

notes.name: Tirthahalli - Purandarasa
notes.note: Shivamogga district, Karnataka. Purandaradasa, c. 1484-1564. Called the father of Carnatic music, the man who turned a performing art into a teachable system. Janti varisai and alankaras, set in the Mayamalavagowla raga.

notes.name: Tirunelveli
notes.note: The Tirunelveli region of southern Tamil Nadu. Broadly Mesolithic and running into the later Holocene. The type-region of the teri microlithic industry, the distinctive Mesolithic of the far south. The teris are fossil dunes of red.

notes.name: Tirupati
notes.note: Tirumala, above the town of Tirupati, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh. The Venkateshvara temple is attested by Pallava inscriptions from the 9th century and endowed successively by the Cholas. The richest temple in India, and the standard case study for the temple as an economic institution.

notes.name: Tiruvakkarai
notes.note: Villupuram district, Tamil Nadu, about 20 km from Puducherry. Palaeolithic surface finds within a Miocene fossil-bearing formation. The locality is best known for petrified wood fossils roughly 20 million years old.

notes.name: Tripuri
notes.note: Tewar, ancient Tripuri, near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh. An early historic settlement with Satavahana and later occupation. The Kalachuri capital, and the origin of an era used across central India. The Kalachuri or Chedi era, reckoned from 248 CE.

notes.name: Tuticorin
notes.note: Thoothukudi, on the Gulf of Mannar coast of southern Tamil Nadu. Mesolithic microlithic scatters on the coastal teri dunes. A coastal Mesolithic locality, and the point at which the teri dune sites meet the sea.

notes.name: Uch
notes.note: Bahawalpur district, Punjab, Pakistan. An ancient site sometimes identified with an Alexandrian foundation on the Indus. The second pole of the Suhrawardi order, and the site of some of the finest glazed-tile architecture in the subcontinent.

notes.name: Udayagiri (Vidisha)
notes.note: Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh. Gupta period. The earliest datable Hindu cave temples in India, and the birthplace of the classical Gupta iconographic programme. The colossal Varaha panel in Cave 5 shows Vishnu as the boar lifting Bhudevi from the cosmic ocean.

notes.name: Udaigiri Khandagiri
notes.note: The twin hills of Udayagiri and Khandagiri, about 6 km west of Bhubaneswar. Generally 1st century BCE. The earliest Jaina rock-cut monastic complex in India, and the physical expression of Kharavela's patronage.

notes.name: Udupi
notes.note: Coastal Karnataka. C. 1238-1317 CE. The seat of Dvaita Vedanta, the systematic dualist answer to Shankara's Advaita, and the source of the Kannada devotional tradition. Madhva argued for an absolute and permanent distinction between the individual soul and Brahman.

notes.name: Ujjain
notes.note: Ujjayini, on the right bank of the Shipra, Madhya Pradesh. Period I begins c. 700 BCE with black-and-red ware behind a massive mud rampart. The largest and earliest urban defence work in central India, and a manufacturing city rather than an agrarian capital.

notes.name: Undavalli Caves
notes.note: Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh. Associated with the Vishnukundin dynasty. A four-storeyed rock-cut temple, the tallest such excavation in the south, and a clear record of a Buddhist site passing into Brahmanical use.

notes.name: Uthiramerur
notes.note: Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, in the Palar basin south-west of Kanchipuram. Founded as a brahmadeya under the Pallavas in the 8th century. The most detailed surviving account of village self-government in the ancient world, effectively the written constitution of the Chola village assembly.

notes.name: Utnoor
notes.note: Utnur, Adilabad district, Telangana, on the Deccan plateau in the upper Godavari basin. A South Indian Neolithic ashmound excavated by F. R. Allchin in 1957. The dig that settled a century of speculation about the Deccan ashmounds.

notes.name: Vaishali
notes.note: Basarh, Vaishali district, Bihar. D. B. Spooner (1913-14), Krishna Deva and Vijayakanta Mishra (1950). The best-documented gana-sangha in Indian history, and the site of the earliest excavated Buddhist stupa. Government was by an assembly of Licchavi rajas, not a king.

notes.name: Vallabhi
notes.note: Vala, Bhavnagar district, Gujarat, in eastern Saurashtra near the Gulf of Khambhat. C. 475-775 CE. The great centre of Hinayana learning, and the western counterweight to Mahayana Nalanda. Its mahavihara taught the Sthaviravada and Sammitiya doctrines along with nitishastra (statecraft), law and philosophy.

notes.name: Varanasi
notes.note: On the left bank of the Ganga between the Varuna and the Assi. Rajghat excavated by Banaras Hindu University under A. K. Narain and T. N. Roy from 1957. Among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

notes.name: Varanasi - Ramananda, Kabir, Rai Ravidas
notes.note: On the left bank of the Ganga where the river turns north. The 15th and early 16th centuries. The place where north Indian bhakti became a movement that crossed caste and religion, and where the nirguna tradition took shape.

notes.name: Vatsagumla
notes.note: Washim, ancient Vatsagulma, Washim district, Maharashtra, on the Penganga watershed in southern Vidarbha. In the later 4th century CE and ruling until the early 6th. The court that paid for the later caves at Ajanta, the most consequential act of patronage in Indian art history.

notes.name: Veerapuram
notes.note: Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh, on the right bank of the Krishna near Nandikotkur. A neolithic level. A type site for the cultural sequence of the Krishna valley, chosen and published precisely for its unbroken column.

notes.name: Vengi
notes.note: Pedavegi, ancient Vengi, Eluru district, Andhra Pradesh. A centre from the Mauryan period. The seat of the Eastern Chalukyas, whose dynastic marriage into the Cholas reshaped south Indian politics and created Telugu literature.

notes.name: Vidisha
notes.note: At the confluence of the Betwa (Vetravati) and the Bes, Madhya Pradesh. D. R. Bhandarkar (1913-15) and M. D. Khare (1963-65). Carries the earliest epigraphic evidence for Bhagavata worship, and the earliest named craft guild in Indian art.

notes.name: Vijayapura or Bijapur
notes.note: Long known as Bijapur, northern Karnataka. Capital of the Adil Shahi sultanate from 1490. The most accomplished architecture of the Deccan sultanates, and a court whose religious eclecticism rivalled Akbar's.

notes.name: Vikramshila
notes.note: Antichak, Bhagalpur district, Bihar. C. 783-820 CE. The leading centre of Vajrayana learning in India, and the source from which Buddhism was re-established in Tibet. The plan is a square monastery of 208 cells around a courtyard.

notes.name: Vilinam
notes.note: Vizhinjam, Thiruvananthapuram district, Kerala. Prominent from about the 8th to the 10th centuries CE. The seat of the Ays, the third power of the far south, and the harbour that its geography made worth fighting for.

notes.name: Viratnagar
notes.note: Bairat (Viratnagar), Jaipur district, Rajasthan. The Buddhist monastery and circular temple on Bijak-ki-Pahari are Mauryan. The earliest free-standing structural Buddhist shrine in India, and the only Ashokan edict that names Buddhist scripture.

notes.name: Vrindavan
notes.note: Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh. An ancient tirtha that was effectively refounded in the 16th century. The physical centre of Krishna bhakti, and a case of a sacred landscape being deliberately reconstructed.

notes.name: Warangal
notes.note: Telangana, on the Deccan plateau in the upper Krishna-Godavari interfluve. Capital of the Kakatiyas from the 12th century. The Kakatiya capital, with one of the very few women to rule an Indian kingdom in her own right.

notes.name: Woraiyur
notes.note: Uraiyur, now a quarter of Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu. C. 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE. The seat of the early Cholas before Thanjavur, and the cotton town of the Sangam economy.

notes.name: Yerragudi
notes.note: Near Gooty in Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh. C. 257-256 BCE, c. 258-257 BCE. The only site in the empire carrying both the Major and the Minor Rock Edicts. Because both sets appear on one rock.
